A suspicious artifact that was downloaded but never executed requires investigation of how the tooling handled it. Installation or import introduces additional questions about code execution and available credentials. Keep these stages distinct in the incident record. If unknown code ran in a privileged environment, stop using that environment for further secrets or releases. Preserve the relevant logs and artifacts, assess what was reachable, and follow the affected platform’s incident procedures. Deleting the dependency line does not establish that its code had no effect. The enduring control is an accountable installation path: a justified dependency, verified project identity, reviewed artifact set and a constrained execution environment. The agent can keep suggesting ways to finish the job. The installer should continue requiring a decision about the actual software it is about to run. items.summary_html:
A practical guide to invented dependencies, registry identity and reviewed artifacts, with an offline Python exercise.A plausible package name is a starting point for review, not permission to install its code.

A coding assistant cannot find a convenient parser for your import job. It proposes a dependency, adds an import and offers to install the package so it can finish testing. The name looks plausible. A registry search even finds something with the same spelling.

Before the command runs, someone still needs to establish who publishes that package, where it will be downloaded from and why that specific artifact belongs in the project. A successful lookup answers only one of those questions.

This lesson uses a fictional dependency called beagle-demo-parser. It is a teaching label, not a recommendation to find or install a real package. We will inspect the path from suggestion to installation, distinguish a name from an approved artifact, and run a local check that rejects unreviewed changes without downloading anything.

An invented name can become a real installation target

A package hallucination occurs when generated code refers to a dependency that does not exist in the relevant ecosystem at the time it is checked. Slopsquatting describes the associated attack pattern: someone registers a name that models are likely to suggest and relies on a later developer or agent to install that package.

The USENIX Security 2025 study We Have a Package for You! evaluated 16 models and generated 576,000 code samples across Python and JavaScript. Its authors documented fabricated package names and examined whether suggestions recur. This establishes a measured failure mode in that study’s models and prompts. It does not give the current compromise rate of coding agents, or prove that every nonexistent recommendation is an attack. Source: the authors’ USENIX publication.

The timing explains why existence alone is an inadequate defense. A model can invent a name on Monday. An attacker can register it on Tuesday. A developer repeating the task on Wednesday can find a real package, even though the recommendation did not originate from knowledge of that publisher’s software. The authors describe that attack sequence in their accompanying explanation. Source: USENIX author article.

There are other routes to the wrong package. A misspelled name may select a lookalike. A private dependency may resolve from an unintended public source. A legitimate project can also ship a compromised release. These cases have different causes, so the review should establish the chosen artifact’s identity rather than merely classify the spelling mistake.

Review the dependency proposal before making it executable

For the fictional import job, ask what the proposed library does that the existing code or standard library cannot. A small, routine transformation may need no new dependency. Removing unnecessary installation is useful because it removes an entire software-trust decision from this task.

When a dependency is justified, check its identity using the project’s own documentation and the relevant registry. Compare the distribution name, maintained repository, release history and documented installation method. A README inside the candidate package is a claim from its publisher, not independent proof that it is the project you intended.

Use the term distribution name carefully in Python. The name passed to an installer can differ from the name used in an import statement. Python's packaging documentation explicitly distinguishes those concepts, so do not infer an install command solely by copying the import token. Source: Python Packaging User Guide.

For an organization, the review should connect the candidate to a maintained dependency policy. That policy may already define approved registries, allowed namespaces, reviewed versions and who can authorize a new package. An agent proposing a dependency should not also be able to edit the policy that approves it.

Check the publisher and source, pin reviewed artifacts, and inspect the full dependency change before installation.

A useful proposal includes the purpose of the dependency, the exact version, its source and the dependency changes it introduces. Review the lockfile as well as the line added to the top-level manifest. The direct package is only the first part of the code being admitted.

Installation can execute code before your test begins

It is easy to treat installation as a preliminary step before execution. Package managers do not always preserve that distinction.

npm documents lifecycle hooks that run during installation, including preinstall, install and postinstall. Its ignore-scripts option suppresses package scripts for installation, but explicitly requested script commands still run their named script. The setting is a specific control, not a general sandbox. Sources: npm's scripts documentation and npm ci.

For Python, pip’s secure-install guidance recommends hash-checking mode and disallowing source distributions where appropriate. Building a source distribution can involve executing build-system code. A wheel avoids that source-build step, but code from the installed package can still run when imported or used. Source: pip secure installs.

This is why our review happens before granting a coding agent an unrestricted installation tool. A credential-free disposable environment limits what an unknown dependency can reach during assessment. It should also have an explicit network policy and resource limits; an empty working directory alone does not isolate the host.

For an already reviewed npm project, a restricted validation run might begin with:

npm ci --ignore-scripts

This is an installation command and can contact configured registries. It is shown as an example for a disposable review environment, not as part of the offline exercise below. npm ci requires a lockfile and fails when the manifest and lockfile disagree. It does not certify the locked packages as trustworthy. Source: npm ci.

Some legitimate packages need a build hook. Investigate that requirement, review the hook and allow it deliberately in the appropriate environment. Disabling a control globally to get a green build changes the security decision for every dependency in that run.

Learn what a hash actually establishes

A cryptographic digest identifies bytes. When a trusted approval records a digest, comparing the downloaded artifact with that value can detect substitution or corruption. Matching the digest does not establish that the approved artifact is benign.

If the same unreviewed agent supplies both the package and the expected digest, it can make the comparison pass by hashing whatever it chose. The expected value must come from a reviewed record outside the agent’s write authority.

pip’s hash-checking mode requires exact requirements and hashes for the dependency set, including dependencies of dependencies. Its documentation explains why partial coverage leaves a gap. Use the package manager’s supported mechanism rather than inventing a text comparison around an installer command. Source: pip secure installs.

Name normalization matters as well. Python distribution names are compared after lowercasing and replacing runs of hyphens, underscores and periods with a hyphen. Beagle_Demo.Parser and beagle-demo-parser therefore represent the same normalized distribution name in this exercise. Treating them as unrelated packages can break a policy check. Source: Python packaging name normalization.

Existence, publisher identity, artifact integrity and execution safety answer different questions.Run an offline artifact check

The following Python 3.10+ program uses only the standard library. Its artifact is a short byte string, not an installable package. Its registry address ends in .invalid, and the program never resolves or contacts it.

The approved record is fixed by the exercise. The proposed dependency is allowed to vary. The check accepts only the reviewed identity and the reviewed bytes, including equivalent normalized spelling.

Save it as dependency_demo.py:

"""Check a fictional dependency against a trusted local approval. No installs."""
from dataclasses import dataclass, replace
from hashlib import sha256
import re
def normalize_name(name: str) -> str:
    if type(name) is not str or not re.fullmatch(
        r"[A-Za-z0-9](?:[A-Za-z0-9._-]*[A-Za-z0-9])?", name
    ):
        raise ValueError("Invalid distribution name")
    return re.sub(r"[-_.]+", "-", name).lower()

@dataclass(frozen=True)
class Dependency:
    name: str
    version: str
    registry: str
    digest: str

ARTIFACT = b"BEAGLE TEACHING FIXTURE ONLY; NOT AN INSTALLABLE PACKAGE\n"
APPROVED = Dependency(
    "beagle-demo-parser", "1.0.0", "https://registry.example.invalid/simple",
    sha256(ARTIFACT).hexdigest(),
)

def check(candidate: Dependency, artifact: bytes) -> bool:
    # APPROVED is reviewed policy, not data supplied by the coding agent.
    try:
        same_name = normalize_name(candidate.name) == normalize_name(APPROVED.name)
    except (ValueError, TypeError):
        return False
    return (
        same_name
        and candidate.version == APPROVED.version
        and candidate.registry == APPROVED.registry
        and candidate.digest == APPROVED.digest
        and sha256(artifact).hexdigest() == APPROVED.digest
    )

def main() -> None:
    trials = [
        ("approved artifact", APPROVED, ARTIFACT, True),
        ("normalized spelling", replace(APPROVED, name="Beagle_Demo.Parser"),
         ARTIFACT, True),
        ("different package", replace(APPROVED, name="beagle-demo-parser-pro"),
         ARTIFACT, False),
        ("different version", replace(APPROVED, version="9.9.9"), ARTIFACT, False),
        ("different registry", replace(APPROVED, registry="https://other.invalid"),
         ARTIFACT, False),
        ("changed bytes", APPROVED, ARTIFACT + b"changed", False),
    ]
    for label, candidate, artifact, expected in trials:
        result = check(candidate, artifact)
        if result != expected:
            raise AssertionError(f"Unexpected decision: {label}")
        print(f"{label}: {'ACCEPT' if result else 'BLOCK'}")

if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

Run:

python3 dependency_demo.py

Expected output:

approved artifact: ACCEPT
normalized spelling: ACCEPT
different package: BLOCK
different version: BLOCK
different registry: BLOCK
changed bytes: BLOCK

The accompanying tests also change the proposed digest to match altered bytes. That request still fails because the separately held approved record did not change.

This program demonstrates an approval comparison for one fictional artifact. It does not scan malware, resolve real dependencies, verify a publisher or prevent a package from behaving badly after import. A production dependency pipeline must cover the full resolved set and ensure the bytes checked are the bytes installed. Checking a file and later installing a newly downloaded file would reintroduce a gap.

Ask what the lockfile did and did not promise

A lockfile helps keep a dependency graph reproducible. A reviewed graph gives you something concrete to compare against later changes. It does not establish that every resolved package is safe, or that the original review was correct.

For this exercise’s workflow, keep the approval boundary outside the agent-editable project. The agent can propose changes to the manifest and lockfile, but a separate review decides whether those changes become the approved build input. Do not let a passing test automatically approve its own new dependencies.

Inspect source changes, new versions and added transitive packages. Check whether a private dependency can resolve from a second source. pip explicitly warns that using --extra-index-url to find private packages can expose a dependency-confusion risk. The resolver's behavior must match the source policy you intended. Source: pip install reference.

Some teams use an internal proxy or artifact repository to enforce that policy. Such a service is useful only if its routing and admission rules are configured deliberately. A cache that accepts everything from the public internet should not be described as a reviewed package catalog.

For build actions, GitHub recommends pinning third-party actions to full commit hashes and verifying that a chosen commit belongs to the intended repository. That is another application of the same identity question: a short label or mutable tag is not a complete artifact identity. Source: GitHub Actions secure-use reference.

Test your coding workflow before an unexpected dependency arrives

Create a disposable project with a known dependency policy. Start with a task that can be completed without new packages, then a task for which one already approved package is available. Confirm that both legitimate paths still work.

Next, propose a fictional unapproved package without installing it. The workflow should stop at the review boundary and report what approval is missing. Repeat with an unreviewed version of an approved package and with the same name routed to a different registry.

Test whether the agent can alter the expected digest or lockfile in the approval store. It may be permitted to edit its proposal, but that edit must not silently modify the policy against which the proposal is checked.

Use a harmless local package fixture to test lifecycle-script handling in an isolated environment. The script can write a unique marker to the disposable working directory. Observe whether installation runs it, whether the script suppression setting is applied and whether the workflow can bypass that setting through another command. Do not run unknown registry packages to make this test realistic.

Test new names, versions, sources and install hooks in a disposable environment without credentials.

Finally, compare the resolved dependency set with the approved one. Record the package-manager version, configuration, lockfile and artifact identifiers. A clean installation in one configuration is not evidence about a different machine that uses another registry or enables lifecycle scripts.

Respond to the evidence you have

An invented name that was never installed is a rejected proposal. A suspicious artifact that was downloaded but never executed requires investigation of how the tooling handled it. Installation or import introduces additional questions about code execution and available credentials. Keep these stages distinct in the incident record.

If unknown code ran in a privileged environment, stop using that environment for further secrets or releases. Preserve the relevant logs and artifacts, assess what was reachable, and follow the affected platform’s incident procedures. Deleting the dependency line does not establish that its code had no effect.

The enduring control is an accountable installation path: a justified dependency, verified project identity, reviewed artifact set and a constrained execution environment. The agent can keep suggesting ways to finish the job. The installer should continue requiring a decision about the actual software it is about to run.

  2. Source: USENIX author article

  4. Sources: npm’s scripts documentation
  5. npm ci
  6. Source: pip secure installs

items.title: From CI/CD to AgenticOps: Inside OpenAI Work Cloud
items.summary: DevOps and platform engineers are moving from operators to governors. Software engineers are already well down that path. For the past several months, OpenAI Work has been part of my daily engineering routine. Over time, I stopped thinking of it as an AI assistant and started seeing something structurally different: an emerging agentic engineering environment capable of assuming much of the reasoning and execution work traditionally performed by software, DevOps, and platform engineers. Are these professions already “dead” as we knew them? I think so. But you be the judge — comments are welcome. At a Glance In July 2026, OpenAI launched ChatGPT Work , an autonomous enterprise AI agent powered by their flagship GPT-5.6 Sol model family. In this brief, I evaluate the OpenAI Work Cloud architecture and assess how far its execution model overlaps with work traditionally performed by Senior Software Engineers, Senior DevOps / Platform Engineers, and Senior Solution / Enterprise Architects . The architecture goes well beyond conversational assistance. It combines persistent context, task orchestration, specialized sub-agents, integrated development and browser tooling, isolated execution environments, task state and scheduling, retries, approvals, deployment capabilities, and managed infrastructure within a single agentic work environment. The significance is not that Work can simply generate code. It can take a high-level objective, decompose it, assign work to specialized agents, modify software, provision its working environment, execute and test code, inspect failures, revise the implementation, interact with external systems, and continue toward completion within defined security and approval boundaries. That places Work Cloud much closer to an autonomous engineering environment than to a conventional AI assistant agent. In practical terms, it begins to absorb substantial portions of the work historically performed by software engineers, DevOps engineers, platform engineers, and technical architects. The architectural shift is straightforward: Traditional automation executes instructions. Agentic automation increasingly interprets objectives, decides what work is required, executes it, evaluates the result, and adjusts its own course. That is the basis of the AgenticOps model examined in this brief, and a concept I have been developing and writing about publicly since early 2025. 🏗️ Architectural Core Pillars 1. Dynamic Model Layer & Multi-Agent Orchestration The Work architecture substantially automates the manual decomposition and coordination of complex work. Task Orchestrator / Lead Agent: Receives the user’s objective, interprets available persistent context, develops a plan, breaks the work into steps, coordinates execution, monitors progress, and handles failures. Model Routing: The depicted model layer allows different reasoning capabilities to be selected per task or step based on complexity, reasoning requirements, and availability. The supplied architecture shows models ranging from heavier reasoning to lightweight execution. Specialized Sub-Agents: The orchestrator coordinates sub-agents for functions such as coding, research, testing, and deployment . These agents share tools and workspace resources while remaining coordinated through the execution environment. The functional effect resembles a technical team operating under a lead engineer: the orchestrator maintains the overall objective while specialized workers execute bounded portions of the plan. The architecture therefore performs some functions traditionally associated with a Principal Engineer, Technical Lead, or Solution Architect : decomposition, delegation, sequencing, technical decision-making, validation, and synthesis. 2. Native Tooling Layer & Secure Execution Environment Work Cloud integrates much of the engineering workspace directly into the agent runtime. Ephemeral Task Workspace: Each task can receive isolated compute, temporary storage, filesystem access, controlled networking, package installation, and process execution. Development Tooling: Agents can work with repositories, Git operations, code search and editing, pull requests, issues, shell commands, Python, Node.js, and other development utilities. Testing and Repair: Testing is not merely a terminal pipeline stage. The agent can inspect failures, reason about their cause, modify the implementation, and rerun validation. Browser Automation: The Web & Browser layer provides access to web search, live sites, managed browser interaction, screenshots, and form-based workflows. Deployment: The architecture includes a dedicated deployment surface, including web application deployment and Cloudflare targets. Integrations: Connected systems such as Gmail, Calendar, Contacts, plugins, and MCP resources extend the environment beyond local files and code. The important change is not simply that these tools exist in one place. It is that the agent can reason across them as part of one execution loop . 3. Task State, Scheduling & Failure Recovery The Execution Services layer gives Work Cloud characteristics of an operational platform rather than a one-shot assistant. It includes: Task state and scheduling Sub-agent coordination Tool routing and permissions Error handling and retries Live progress and logs Result assembly This makes possible a broader execution pattern: This closed reasoning loop is a major departure from conventional automation. A traditional CI/CD pipeline generally executes a predefined sequence and reports failure. An agentic execution environment can potentially interpret the failure, determine what must change, modify the implementation, and execute the validation again . 🛡️ Integrated Safety, Security & Governance The architecture places governance inside the execution environment rather than treating autonomy as unrestricted authority. It includes: Permissions & approvals for actions requiring user confirmation Tool allow/deny lists Content and action safety checks Audit logs Task isolation Controlled networking Tool routing and permission enforcement The important principle is: Autonomy does not imply unlimited authority. An agent may autonomously plan, edit, test, diagnose, and retry while still being constrained from performing privileged or irreversible actions without explicit authorization. This is the basis for trusted AgenticOps. 📊 Engineering Capability Matrix 🧑‍💻 Software Engineering Chat with the agent — Yes ChatGPT Frontend Conversation serves as the high-level control interface and can transition directly from discussion into execution. Interpret high-level objectives — Yes Task Orchestrator The system converts user intent into an executable plan rather than requiring every engineering step to be prescribed manually. Decompose complex work — Yes Task Orchestrator / Sub-agents Complex tasks can be divided into sequential or parallel activities and coordinated across specialized agents. Access GitHub — Yes Development Tooling Repository operations include code access, search and editing, Git operations, pull requests, and issue interaction. Create architecture — Yes Lead Agent / Productivity Tools The environment can produce architectural designs, technical documentation, diagrams, implementation plans, codebase structures, and working prototypes. Build a development environment — Yes Secure Cloud Workspace It can establish directories, install dependencies and packages, configure development tools, and prepare task-specific workspaces on demand. Execute code — Yes Runtime & Files The execution environment supports shell commands, Python, Node.js, filesystem operations, package installation, and process control inside an isolated workspace. Run tests — Yes Testing Sub-Agent / Runtime Tests, linters, type checks, and other validation steps can be executed directly within the working environment. Diagnose and repair failed tests — Yes Task Orchestrator / Testing Sub-Agent / Logs The system can inspect a failure, reason about its cause, modify the implementation, and rerun validation rather than simply stopping at a failed build. Commit changes and create pull requests — Yes GitHub / Development Tooling Source changes can participate directly in Git-based engineering workflows. Pull-request-based integration remains the safer pattern for production repositories. ⚙️ Operations & Execution Use cloud browsers — Yes Web & Browser Managed browser access supports live websites, interaction, screenshots, web research, and form-based workflows. Authentication and site-specific restrictions may still affect execution. Deploy applications — Yes Sites Deployment The depicted architecture includes application build and deployment capabilities, including Cloudflare deployment paths. Maintain execution state — Yes Task State & Scheduler Active task state is maintained across the execution process rather than requiring every step to be reconstructed from scratch. Run scheduled work — Yes Task State & Scheduler Work can be initiated through scheduled or recurring execution rather than requiring a new interactive prompt for every run. Retry failed work — Yes Error Handling & Retries Failure handling is part of the execution environment. A failed operation can feed back into diagnosis, modification, and another execution attempt. Use external applications and services — Yes Integrations / MCP Agents can extend their reach through connected applications and standardized tool interfaces rather than operating only on local files. 🛡️ Context, Security & Governance Maintain persistent context — Yes Projects / Library / Memory / Connected Apps Longer-lived context can provide files, instructions, goals, knowledge, preferences, and connected-system information independently of the temporary execution workspace. Operate autonomously — Yes, within delegated scope Orchestration / Scheduler / Tooling Work can proceed for extended periods without continuous human interaction, provided the required capabilities and permissions have already been delegated. In my experience, 50–60min sessions were not uncommon. A rule of thumb: split your project into weekly deliverables and let the Work work it out in chunks. Operate with unlimited privileged authority — No Safety, Security & Governance Privileged, destructive, or sensitive actions remain constrained by credentials, permissions, approvals, safety rules, and the authority available to the environment. An agent can be highly autonomous in planning, implementation, diagnosis, and validation while still operating inside explicit security boundaries. 🤖 Automation & AgenticOps Boundary Create and evolve CI/CD pipelines— Yes Agentic Engineering / Development Tooling The Work environment can generate and modify the Dockerfiles, workflows, infrastructure-as-code, tests, deployment definitions, and policy controls that make up a deterministic delivery pipeline. This moves pipeline engineering itself into the agentic domain. Operate CI/CD autonomously — Yes Orchestration / Development / Deployment Work agents can invoke the pipeline they create, monitor its execution, interpret failures, modify the implementation or pipeline configuration, rerun validation, and continue toward deployment within defined authority boundaries. That produces an important distinction: AgenticOps makes much of the human engineering traditionally required to create, operate, troubleshoot, and evolve CI/CD disappear. The underlying tools do not disappear. What changes is the entity operating them: Human engineer → Git / CI / IaC / Cloud / Monitoring becomes increasingly: Human intent and governance → Agentic control plane → Git / CI / IaC / Cloud / Monitoring This is where Work Cloud begins to resemble an autonomous engineering environment rather than simply an AI assistant . 🔄 Traditional DevOps vs. AgenticOps The critical change is that the reasoning loop itself becomes automated . Git, tests, CI, cloud infrastructure, policy engines, and deployment systems do not disappear. The entity operating them changes. The human DevOps engineer who traditionally designs, assembles, maintains, troubleshoots, and operates that pipeline is increasingly optional. The lifecycle is more accurately described in phases: Phase 1 — Work builds the delivery system Work can generate and configure: Dockerfiles and container builds GitHub/GitLab workflows CI/CD stages Terraform/IaC Ansible playbooks deployment manifests tests and validation steps security scans and policy gates environment configuration So the agent is already performing work traditionally done by DevOps/platform engineers. items.summary_html:
DevOps and platform engineers are moving from operators to governors. Software engineers are already well down that path.

For the past several months, OpenAI Work has been part of my daily engineering routine. Over time, I stopped thinking of it as an AI assistant and started seeing something structurally different: an emerging agentic engineering environment capable of assuming much of the reasoning and execution work traditionally performed by software, DevOps, and platform engineers.

Are these professions already “dead” as we knew them? I think so. But you be the judge — comments are welcome.

At a Glance

In July 2026, OpenAI launched ChatGPT Work, an autonomous enterprise AI agent powered by their flagship GPT-5.6 Sol model family. In this brief, I evaluate the OpenAI Work Cloud architecture and assess how far its execution model overlaps with work traditionally performed by Senior Software Engineers, Senior DevOps / Platform Engineers, and Senior Solution / Enterprise Architects.

The architecture goes well beyond conversational assistance. It combines persistent context, task orchestration, specialized sub-agents, integrated development and browser tooling, isolated execution environments, task state and scheduling, retries, approvals, deployment capabilities, and managed infrastructure within a single agentic work environment.

The significance is not that Work can simply generate code. It can take a high-level objective, decompose it, assign work to specialized agents, modify software, provision its working environment, execute and test code, inspect failures, revise the implementation, interact with external systems, and continue toward completion within defined security and approval boundaries.

That places Work Cloud much closer to an autonomous engineering environment than to a conventional AI assistant agent. In practical terms, it begins to absorb substantial portions of the work historically performed by software engineers, DevOps engineers, platform engineers, and technical architects.

The architectural shift is straightforward:

Traditional automation executes instructions. Agentic automation increasingly interprets objectives, decides what work is required, executes it, evaluates the result, and adjusts its own course.

That is the basis of the AgenticOps model examined in this brief, and a concept I have been developing and writing about publicly since early 2025.

🏗️ Architectural Core Pillars1. Dynamic Model Layer & Multi-Agent Orchestration

The Work architecture substantially automates the manual decomposition and coordination of complex work.

  • Task Orchestrator / Lead Agent: Receives the user’s objective, interprets available persistent context, develops a plan, breaks the work into steps, coordinates execution, monitors progress, and handles failures.
  • Model Routing: The depicted model layer allows different reasoning capabilities to be selected per task or step based on complexity, reasoning requirements, and availability. The supplied architecture shows models ranging from heavier reasoning to lightweight execution.
  • Specialized Sub-Agents: The orchestrator coordinates sub-agents for functions such as coding, research, testing, and deployment. These agents share tools and workspace resources while remaining coordinated through the execution environment.

The functional effect resembles a technical team operating under a lead engineer: the orchestrator maintains the overall objective while specialized workers execute bounded portions of the plan.

The architecture therefore performs some functions traditionally associated with a Principal Engineer, Technical Lead, or Solution Architect: decomposition, delegation, sequencing, technical decision-making, validation, and synthesis.

2. Native Tooling Layer & Secure Execution Environment

Work Cloud integrates much of the engineering workspace directly into the agent runtime.

  • Ephemeral Task Workspace: Each task can receive isolated compute, temporary storage, filesystem access, controlled networking, package installation, and process execution.
  • Development Tooling: Agents can work with repositories, Git operations, code search and editing, pull requests, issues, shell commands, Python, Node.js, and other development utilities.
  • Testing and Repair: Testing is not merely a terminal pipeline stage. The agent can inspect failures, reason about their cause, modify the implementation, and rerun validation.
  • Browser Automation: The Web & Browser layer provides access to web search, live sites, managed browser interaction, screenshots, and form-based workflows.
  • Deployment: The architecture includes a dedicated deployment surface, including web application deployment and Cloudflare targets.
  • Integrations: Connected systems such as Gmail, Calendar, Contacts, plugins, and MCP resources extend the environment beyond local files and code.

The important change is not simply that these tools exist in one place. It is that the agent can reason across them as part of one execution loop.

3. Task State, Scheduling & Failure Recovery

The Execution Services layer gives Work Cloud characteristics of an operational platform rather than a one-shot assistant.

It includes:

  • Task state and scheduling
  • Sub-agent coordination
  • Tool routing and permissions
  • Error handling and retries
  • Live progress and logs
  • Result assembly

This makes possible a broader execution pattern:

This closed reasoning loop is a major departure from conventional automation.

A traditional CI/CD pipeline generally executes a predefined sequence and reports failure.

An agentic execution environment can potentially interpret the failure, determine what must change, modify the implementation, and execute the validation again.

🛡️ Integrated Safety, Security & Governance

The architecture places governance inside the execution environment rather than treating autonomy as unrestricted authority.

It includes:

  • Permissions & approvals for actions requiring user confirmation
  • Tool allow/deny lists
  • Content and action safety checks
  • Audit logs
  • Task isolation
  • Controlled networking
  • Tool routing and permission enforcement

The important principle is:

Autonomy does not imply unlimited authority. An agent may autonomously plan, edit, test, diagnose, and retry while still being constrained from performing privileged or irreversible actions without explicit authorization.

This is the basis for trusted AgenticOps.

📊 Engineering Capability Matrix🧑‍💻 Software Engineering

Chat with the agent — Yes
ChatGPT Frontend
Conversation serves as the high-level control interface and can transition directly from discussion into execution.

Interpret high-level objectives — Yes
Task Orchestrator
The system converts user intent into an executable plan rather than requiring every engineering step to be prescribed manually.

Decompose complex work — Yes
Task Orchestrator / Sub-agents
Complex tasks can be divided into sequential or parallel activities and coordinated across specialized agents.

Access GitHub — Yes
Development Tooling
Repository operations include code access, search and editing, Git operations, pull requests, and issue interaction.

Create architecture — Yes
Lead Agent / Productivity Tools
The environment can produce architectural designs, technical documentation, diagrams, implementation plans, codebase structures, and working prototypes.

Build a development environment — Yes
Secure Cloud Workspace
It can establish directories, install dependencies and packages, configure development tools, and prepare task-specific workspaces on demand.

Execute code — Yes
Runtime & Files
The execution environment supports shell commands, Python, Node.js, filesystem operations, package installation, and process control inside an isolated workspace.

Run tests — Yes
Testing Sub-Agent / Runtime
Tests, linters, type checks, and other validation steps can be executed directly within the working environment.

Diagnose and repair failed tests — Yes
Task Orchestrator / Testing Sub-Agent / Logs
The system can inspect a failure, reason about its cause, modify the implementation, and rerun validation rather than simply stopping at a failed build.

Commit changes and create pull requests — Yes
GitHub / Development Tooling
Source changes can participate directly in Git-based engineering workflows. Pull-request-based integration remains the safer pattern for production repositories.

⚙️ Operations & Execution

Use cloud browsers — Yes
Web & Browser
Managed browser access supports live websites, interaction, screenshots, web research, and form-based workflows. Authentication and site-specific restrictions may still affect execution.

Deploy applications — Yes
Sites Deployment
The depicted architecture includes application build and deployment capabilities, including Cloudflare deployment paths.

Maintain execution state — Yes
Task State & Scheduler
Active task state is maintained across the execution process rather than requiring every step to be reconstructed from scratch.

Run scheduled work — Yes
Task State & Scheduler
Work can be initiated through scheduled or recurring execution rather than requiring a new interactive prompt for every run.

Retry failed work — Yes
Error Handling & Retries
Failure handling is part of the execution environment. A failed operation can feed back into diagnosis, modification, and another execution attempt.

Use external applications and services — Yes
Integrations / MCP
Agents can extend their reach through connected applications and standardized tool interfaces rather than operating only on local files.

🛡️ Context, Security & Governance

Maintain persistent context — Yes
Projects / Library / Memory / Connected Apps
Longer-lived context can provide files, instructions, goals, knowledge, preferences, and connected-system information independently of the temporary execution workspace.

Operate autonomously — Yes, within delegated scope
Orchestration / Scheduler / Tooling
Work can proceed for extended periods without continuous human interaction, provided the required capabilities and permissions have already been delegated. In my experience, 50–60min sessions were not uncommon. A rule of thumb: split your project into weekly deliverables and let the Work work it out in chunks.

Operate with unlimited privileged authority — No
Safety, Security & Governance
Privileged, destructive, or sensitive actions remain constrained by credentials, permissions, approvals, safety rules, and the authority available to the environment.

An agent can be highly autonomous in planning, implementation, diagnosis, and validation while still operating inside explicit security boundaries.
🤖 Automation & AgenticOps Boundary

Create and evolve CI/CD pipelines— Yes
Agentic Engineering / Development Tooling
The Work environment can generate and modify the Dockerfiles, workflows, infrastructure-as-code, tests, deployment definitions, and policy controls that make up a deterministic delivery pipeline. This moves pipeline engineering itself into the agentic domain.

Operate CI/CD autonomously — Yes
Orchestration / Development / Deployment
Work agents can invoke the pipeline they create, monitor its execution, interpret failures, modify the implementation or pipeline configuration, rerun validation, and continue toward deployment within defined authority boundaries.

That produces an important distinction:

AgenticOps makes much of the human engineering traditionally required to create, operate, troubleshoot, and evolve CI/CD disappear.

The underlying tools do not disappear. What changes is the entity operating them:

Human engineer → Git / CI / IaC / Cloud / Monitoring

becomes increasingly:

Human intent and governance → Agentic control plane → Git / CI / IaC / Cloud / Monitoring

This is where Work Cloud begins to resemble an autonomous engineering environment rather than simply an AI assistant.

🔄 Traditional DevOps vs. AgenticOps

The critical change is that the reasoning loop itself becomes automated.

Git, tests, CI, cloud infrastructure, policy engines, and deployment systems do not disappear.

The entity operating them changes. The human DevOps engineer who traditionally designs, assembles, maintains, troubleshoots, and operates that pipeline is increasingly optional.

The lifecycle is more accurately described in phases:

Phase 1 — Work builds the delivery system

Work can generate and configure:

  • Dockerfiles and container builds
  • GitHub/GitLab workflows
  • CI/CD stages
  • Terraform/IaC
  • Ansible playbooks
  • deployment manifests
  • tests and validation steps
  • security scans and policy gates
  • environment configuration

So the agent is already performing work traditionally done by DevOps/platform engineers.

Phase 2 — Work operates the delivery system

Once those deterministic controls exist, Work can:

  • trigger the pipeline;
  • monitor execution;
  • inspect logs;
  • diagnose failures;
  • change code/configuration;
  • rerun failed stages;
  • validate the result;
  • proceed toward deployment;
  • stop at approval boundaries where required.

The deterministic tools become instruments operated by the agent.

Phase 3 — Work evolves the delivery system

When the application or architecture changes, the agent can also modify: CI/CD workflow, Terraform IaC, Dockerfiles, tests, deployment configurations and playbooks, policy checks, and validate the revised delivery system.

That is much closer to what a human platform team traditionally does.

⚙️ AgenticOps Definition
AgenticOps is an operating model in which autonomous agents assume much of the reasoning, coordination, diagnosis, engineering, and execution traditionally performed by DevOps and platform engineers. Human authority is shifting toward governance and compliance oversight.

AI increasingly becomes the reasoning and control layer operating infrastructure automation it engineered

📌 Human Engineering Role AssessmentSenior Software Engineer

Work Cloud overlaps substantially with the execution loop:

requirements → code inspection → implementation → execution → testing → diagnosis → correction → validation → integration

It can therefore automate almost completely the hands-on software-engineering lifecycle.

Human ownership remains important for product intent, organizational judgment, long-term accountability, and risk acceptance.

Senior DevOps / Platform Engineer

The overlap is particularly strong because the architecture combines:

state + scheduling + execution + Git + testing + networking + deployment + permissions + logging + retries

with an adaptive reasoning layer above them.

This is why Work Cloud can reasonably be viewed as approaching an:

Autonomous AgenticOps Platform Engineer

within delegated operational boundaries.

Senior / Principal Architect

The Task Orchestrator performs several functions associated with senior technical leadership:

  • interpreting high-level objectives;
  • decomposing systems and work;
  • selecting implementation paths;
  • coordinating specialized execution;
  • validating outcomes;
  • producing architecture artifacts;
  • maintaining architectural context.

It does not eliminate the broader organizational responsibilities of an Enterprise Architect — portfolio governance, organizational politics, budget authority, regulatory accountability, or long-term business ownership — but it increasingly automates the technical reasoning and implementation portion of that role.

📌 Strategic Conclusion

OpenAI Work Cloud demonstrates a significant change in software and platform engineering.

The important transition is not simply that AI can generate code.

It is that a single agentic environment can combine:

reasoning + planning + coding + research + testing + repair + browser operation + integration + deployment + scheduling + permissions + state + compute

and apply them repeatedly toward an outcome.

Traditional CI/CD automated execution of predefined procedures under the authority of human engineers:

Work Cloud automates creation of such procedures and the reasoning loop surrounding those procedures.

That turns the environment from a collection of developer tools into something closer to an agentic engineering control system.

Instead of spending most of the time manually assembling environments, interpreting routine failures, wiring tools together, and executing repetitive operational procedures, the senior engineer / architect increasingly defines:

  • architectural boundaries and blueprints;
  • security and policy constraints;
  • acceptable authority;
  • quality thresholds;
  • production guardrails;
  • escalation rules;
  • evidence requirements;
  • desired outcomes;
  • budgetary considerations;
  • AI ROI and business value thresholds.

The human role therefore moves upward: from operator toward governor of an autonomous engineering system, while the agentic platform performs a growing portion of solution architecture, design, implementation, testing, deployment, and operations.

The economic implication is difficult to ignore

The cost of AI is already small relative to professional labor for many organizations. Ramp’s July 2026 data shows median AI spending of about $12 per employee per month among businesses in its dataset. Ramp On its own, however, inexpensive AI does not create transformation.

A 2026 INSEAD/Harvard field experiment involving 515 startups provides a more important clue. The firms that were shown how other companies had reorganized their production around AI substantially outperformed the control group on AI use-case discovery, task completion, customer acquisition, and revenue. The tools were not the differentiator. How the organization redesigned work around them was. SSRN

That should have consequences for technology leadership.

If an agentic engineering environment can increasingly write the code, construct the CI/CD machinery, configure the runtime, run the tests, diagnose routine failures, modify the pipeline, and operate the resulting system, then organizations should reconsider what they are actually hiring senior engineers to do.

Interviewing senior software, DevOps, or platform candidates primarily on memorized syntax, hand-written pipeline mechanics, command trivia, or LeetCode-style exercises increasingly tests proficiency in work that machines are already capable of performing.

The scarce human capabilities move elsewhere:

architecture, systems judgment, security, governance, failure analysis, trade-off decisions, accountability, economics, and deciding what should — or should not — be automated.

The question for technology leaders is therefore no longer simply:

How can AI make our existing engineers faster?

It is increasingly:

How should we redesign engineering itself now that agents can perform a substantial part of the work?

That is the architectural significance of Work Cloud — and why it is already remarkably close to the operating model implied by AgenticOps.

items.title: Snowflake AI Cost Optimization: Where the Spend Comes From, How to Detect It, and How to Control It
items.summary: Understanding and controlling costs of Snowflake AI from Cortex AI Inference & Search, through to experimental development, retries and out-of-control workloads. Snowflake AI brings a new complexity to managing costs. Snowflake has traditionally been optimized around warehouse sizes, query performance, auto suspend, storage and pipeline costs. With AI workloads there are some new complexities. An application request could contain many elements including, LLM inference, document fetch, multiple SQL queries and multiple model evaluations. During experimentation a developer could make many AI requests, often without knowing they have created dozens of AI requests. The main issue with Snowflake AI is that it is a credit intensive process and can be a bit of a stealth cost. This makes it hard to track with traditional dashboards. In this article I will discuss: Where do Snowflake AI costs occur? How can we understand what services and workloads are consuming credits? What SQL queries can I run to monitor my AI usage? How can we control unexpected costs? What practices during development can cause hidden costs? 1. Understanding where Snowflake AI costs occur Depending on the feature, deployment type and pricing, there can be a number of costs associated with your AI workloads. Not all AI costs will be warehouse related. There may be multiple costing elements including AI service usage, warehouse compute and additional service costs. Before you start calculating any costs, please check your current pricing documentation for your region, cloud and contract. The credit rate and metering will depend on the feature. 2. AI Cost Monitoring Architecture A good FinOps architecture for AI will allow you to understand where costs are being used, who is using them (project/developer), identify anomalies and allow for the correct remediation. Reference Architecture for AI Consumption Monitoring, Attribution, Anomaly Detection and Remediation. It is important to ensure that your detection and remediation are separated. When you identify an anomaly you should investigate. If you want to automatically cancel production AI workloads you need a higher level of protection. 3. SQL Queries to understand Snowflake AI Costs The queries below utilizeSnowflake Account Usage views. They are a good starting point for building your operational cost monitoring tool. Query 1: Identify total AI-related credits by service SELECT USAGE_DATE, SERVICE_TYPE, SUM(CREDITS_USED) AS CREDITS_USED FROM SNOWFLAKE.ACCOUNT_USAGE.METERING_DAILY_HISTORY WHERE USAGE_DATE >= DATEADD(DAY, -30, CURRENT_DATE()) AND ( SERVICE_TYPE ILIKE '%AI%' OR SERVICE_TYPE ILIKE '%CORTEX%' OR SERVICE_TYPE ILIKE '%COCO%' ) GROUP BY 1, 2 ORDER BY USAGE_DATE DESC, CREDITS_USED DESC; This provides a high-level breakdown of metered AI-related services. Treat the service-name filter as a discovery query, not a complete billing reconciliation: confirm the service types in your account against Snowflake’s current metering documentation. Query 2: Find the most expensive AI functions and models SELECT FUNCTION_NAME, MODEL_NAME, COUNT(DISTINCT QUERY_ID) AS QUERY_COUNT, ROUND(SUM(CREDITS), 4) AS AI_CREDITS FROM SNOWFLAKE.ACCOUNT_USAGE.CORTEX_AI_FUNCTIONS_USAGE_HISTORY WHERE START_TIME >= DATEADD(DAY, -7, CURRENT_TIMESTAMP()) GROUP BY 1, 2 ORDER BY AI_CREDITS DESC; This helps identify which functions and models consume the most AI credits. The view records AI-function credits separately from warehouse credits, and long-running queries can have multiple hourly records. Query 3: Identify expensive individual AI queries SELECT QUERY_ID, MODEL_NAME, FUNCTION_NAME, MIN(START_TIME) AS FIRST_SEEN, MAX(END_TIME) AS LAST_SEEN, SUM(CREDITS) AS AI_CREDITS FROM SNOWFLAKE.ACCOUNT_USAGE.CORTEX_AI_FUNCTIONS_USAGE_HISTORY WHERE START_TIME >= DATEADD(DAY, -7, CURRENT_TIMESTAMP()) GROUP BY 1, 2, 3 ORDER BY AI_CREDITS DESC LIMIT 25; This is particularly useful for finding bulk AI processing queries that invoke a model across many records. Query 4: Identify expensive Cortex Search services SELECT DATABASE_NAME, SCHEMA_NAME, SERVICE_NAME, CONSUMPTION_TYPE, ROUND(SUM(CREDITS), 4) AS CREDITS FROM SNOWFLAKE.ACCOUNT_USAGE.CORTEX_SEARCH_DAILY_USAGE_HISTORY WHERE USAGE_DATE >= DATEADD(DAY, -30, CURRENT_DATE()) GROUP BY 1, 2, 3, 4 ORDER BY CREDITS DESC; The consumption categories distinguish serving, embedding, and batch usage. When combining this view with AI Functions usage, avoid double-counting embedding credits. Query 5: Find developers repeatedly running AI functions First, assign meaningful query tags in your development sessions: ALTER SESSION SET QUERY_TAG = 'project=ai_cost_monitor;env=dev;team=data_engineering'; Then investigate the most expensive AI queries alongside query history: WITH AI_COST AS ( SELECT QUERY_ID, SUM(CREDITS) AS AI_CREDITS FROM SNOWFLAKE.ACCOUNT_USAGE.CORTEX_AI_FUNCTIONS_USAGE_HISTORY WHERE START_TIME >= DATEADD(DAY, -7, CURRENT_TIMESTAMP()) GROUP BY QUERY_ID ) SELECT Q.USER_NAME, Q.QUERY_TAG, COUNT(*) AS QUERY_COUNT, ROUND(SUM(A.AI_CREDITS), 4) AS AI_CREDITS FROM AI_COST A JOIN SNOWFLAKE.ACCOUNT_USAGE.QUERY_HISTORY Q ON A.QUERY_ID = Q.QUERY_ID GROUP BY 1, 2 ORDER BY AI_CREDITS DESC; This attributes AI-function spending to the SQL user and query tag where query-history records are available. It does not necessarily identify the end user behind a shared service account. 4. Detecting unexpected AI spending An effective monitoring system should distinguish a normal increase in usage from an abnormal one. For example, suppose your development environment usually consumes 10 AI credits daily, but suddenly consumes 80. Illustrative AI credit consumption Friday’s eightfold increase deserves investigation, but is not automatically evidence of waste. A simple first step is to compare today’s usage with the previous seven days. WITH DAILY AS ( SELECT USAGE_DATE, SUM(CREDITS_USED) AS CREDITS FROM SNOWFLAKE.ACCOUNT_USAGE.METERING_DAILY_HISTORY WHERE SERVICE_TYPE = 'AI_FUNCTIONS' AND USAGE_DATE >= DATEADD(DAY, -8, CURRENT_DATE()) GROUP BY 1 ), BASELINE AS ( SELECT AVG(CREDITS) AS AVG_CREDITS FROM DAILY WHERE USAGE_DATE BETWEEN DATEADD(DAY, -7, CURRENT_DATE()) AND DATEADD(DAY, -1, CURRENT_DATE()) ) SELECT D.USAGE_DATE, D.CREDITS, B.AVG_CREDITS, ROUND(D.CREDITS / NULLIF(B.AVG_CREDITS, 0), 2) AS BASELINE_MULTIPLIER FROM DAILY D CROSS JOIN BASELINE B WHERE D.USAGE_DATE = CURRENT_DATE(); This example monitors the AI_FUNCTIONS service type. For a complete AI budget, reconcile all applicable AI service types rather than relying on a single category. Daily metering may also be delayed, so use the appropriate feature-specific views for more timely detection. 5. Unexpected AI costs during development Development is one of the easiest places to accumulate AI spending without noticing it. Consider a developer building a product-review classification pipeline. The initial experiment processes 100 customer reviews. Everything works, so the developer runs the same logic against 100,000 records. But the SQL query invokes an AI function once per row. The result is potentially 100,000 model evaluations from a single SQL statement. Here are common development scenarios that create unexpected costs. Example: How a simple SQL statement becomes expensive SELECT REVIEW_ID, AI_SENTIMENT(REVIEW_TEXT) AS SENTIMENT FROM CUSTOMER_REVIEWS; This is straightforward SQL, but processing a large table can generate substantial AI usage. A safer development approach: SELECT REVIEW_ID, AI_SENTIMENT(REVIEW_TEXT) AS SENTIMENT FROM CUSTOMER_REVIEWS WHERE REVIEW_TEXT IS NOT NULL ORDER BY REVIEW_ID LIMIT 100; The second query limits the input to 100 records. It is useful for controlled experimentation, although you should not assume that adding LIMIT to every SQL shape guarantees a corresponding reduction in AI evaluations. For expensive workloads, explicitly materialize the sample before invoking AI. CREATE OR REPLACE TEMP TABLE REVIEW_SAMPLE AS SELECT REVIEW_ID, REVIEW_TEXT FROM CUSTOMER_REVIEWS WHERE REVIEW_TEXT IS NOT NULL ORDER BY REVIEW_ID LIMIT 100; SELECT REVIEW_ID, AI_SENTIMENT(REVIEW_TEXT) AS SENTIMENT FROM REVIEW_SAMPLE; This creates a bounded input dataset before inference begins. 6. A practical cost-control framework I recommend a five-layer approach. Snowflake now documents AI-specific resource and shared budgets, as well as per-user quotas for supported features. Budget actions are periodic rather than instantaneous; quotas can block additional requests more quickly. Suggested development controls For an organization introducing Snowflake AI, I would start with these policies: Every AI workload must have an identifiable owner and environment. Development AI workloads must have defined credit limits. Production deployments require a cost estimate per 1,000 requests or records. Large-scale AI processing requires an approved input-volume threshold. Repeated inference should use persisted results where appropriate. Agentic applications must have retry and tool-execution limits. Cost anomalies should be investigated before automatic remediation is enabled. These controls should be applied based on workload criticality. A research experiment and a customer-facing production application should not have identical enforcement rules. 7. Measuring the cost of AI applications One of the most useful metrics is not simply total credits. It is cost per successful business outcome. For example, suppose a document classification application consumes 120 credits to process 40,000 documents, of which 36,000 are successfully classified. These are illustrative calculations, not observed Snowflake performance. An optimization that reduces total credits but significantly increases classification errors may actually worsen business economics. Track inference cost alongside accuracy, latency, retries, and successful outcomes. 8. Implementation roadmap A practical Snowflake AI FinOps rollout can be organized into four phases. Week 1 — Visibility: Identify all active AI services, establish daily usage reporting, and classify development versus production consumption. Week 2 — Attribution: Add query tags, map service accounts to applications, and create project-level cost reporting. Week 3 — Detection: Establish rolling baselines, unusual-spend alerts, and high-credit query investigations. Week 4 — Controls: Configure applicable budgets and quotas, implement development guardrails, and test escalation procedures. Conclusion: AI cost optimization is an engineering discipline As Snowflake AI adoption grows, cost optimization must extend beyond warehouse sizing and query tuning. AI workloads introduce new consumption patterns: token processing, document extraction, search serving, multi-step agent execution, and repeated development experimentation. The most effective approach is to establish visibility first, identify which workloads drive spending, then introduce controls that preserve useful AI capabilities without allowing uncontrolled consumption. The objective is not to minimize every AI credit. It is to ensure that every AI workload delivers measurable value at a predictable cost. items.summary_html:
Understanding and controlling costs of Snowflake AI from Cortex AI Inference & Search, through to experimental development, retries and out-of-control workloads.

Snowflake AI brings a new complexity to managing costs.

Snowflake has traditionally been optimized around warehouse sizes, query performance, auto suspend, storage and pipeline costs. With AI workloads there are some new complexities.

An application request could contain many elements including, LLM inference, document fetch, multiple SQL queries and multiple model evaluations. During experimentation a developer could make many AI requests, often without knowing they have created dozens of AI requests.

The main issue with Snowflake AI is that it is a credit intensive process and can be a bit of a stealth cost. This makes it hard to track with traditional dashboards.

In this article I will discuss:

  • Where do Snowflake AI costs occur?
  • How can we understand what services and workloads are consuming credits?
  • What SQL queries can I run to monitor my AI usage?
  • How can we control unexpected costs?
  • What practices during development can cause hidden costs?
1. Understanding where Snowflake AI costs occur

Depending on the feature, deployment type and pricing, there can be a number of costs associated with your AI workloads.

Not all AI costs will be warehouse related. There may be multiple costing elements including AI service usage, warehouse compute and additional service costs. Before you start calculating any costs, please check your current pricing documentation for your region, cloud and contract. The credit rate and metering will depend on the feature.

2. AI Cost Monitoring Architecture

A good FinOps architecture for AI will allow you to understand where costs are being used, who is using them (project/developer), identify anomalies and allow for the correct remediation.

Reference Architecture for AI Consumption Monitoring, Attribution, Anomaly Detection and Remediation.

It is important to ensure that your detection and remediation are separated. When you identify an anomaly you should investigate. If you want to automatically cancel production AI workloads you need a higher level of protection.

3. SQL Queries to understand Snowflake AI Costs

The queries below utilizeSnowflake Account Usage views. They are a good starting point for building your operational cost monitoring tool.

Query 1: Identify total AI-related credits by service
SELECT
    USAGE_DATE,
    SERVICE_TYPE,
    SUM(CREDITS_USED) AS CREDITS_USED
FROM SNOWFLAKE.ACCOUNT_USAGE.METERING_DAILY_HISTORY
WHERE USAGE_DATE >= DATEADD(DAY, -30, CURRENT_DATE())
  AND (
      SERVICE_TYPE ILIKE '%AI%'
      OR SERVICE_TYPE ILIKE '%CORTEX%'
      OR SERVICE_TYPE ILIKE '%COCO%'
  )
GROUP BY 1, 2
ORDER BY USAGE_DATE DESC, CREDITS_USED DESC;

This provides a high-level breakdown of metered AI-related services. Treat the service-name filter as a discovery query, not a complete billing reconciliation: confirm the service types in your account against Snowflake’s current metering documentation.

Query 2: Find the most expensive AI functions and models
SELECT
    FUNCTION_NAME,
    MODEL_NAME,
    COUNT(DISTINCT QUERY_ID) AS QUERY_COUNT,
    ROUND(SUM(CREDITS), 4) AS AI_CREDITS
FROM SNOWFLAKE.ACCOUNT_USAGE.CORTEX_AI_FUNCTIONS_USAGE_HISTORY
WHERE START_TIME >= DATEADD(DAY, -7, CURRENT_TIMESTAMP())
GROUP BY 1, 2
ORDER BY AI_CREDITS DESC;

This helps identify which functions and models consume the most AI credits. The view records AI-function credits separately from warehouse credits, and long-running queries can have multiple hourly records.

Query 3: Identify expensive individual AI queries
SELECT
    QUERY_ID,
    MODEL_NAME,
    FUNCTION_NAME,
    MIN(START_TIME) AS FIRST_SEEN,
    MAX(END_TIME) AS LAST_SEEN,
    SUM(CREDITS) AS AI_CREDITS
FROM SNOWFLAKE.ACCOUNT_USAGE.CORTEX_AI_FUNCTIONS_USAGE_HISTORY
WHERE START_TIME >= DATEADD(DAY, -7, CURRENT_TIMESTAMP())
GROUP BY 1, 2, 3
ORDER BY AI_CREDITS DESC
LIMIT 25;

This is particularly useful for finding bulk AI processing queries that invoke a model across many records.

Query 4: Identify expensive Cortex Search services
SELECT
    DATABASE_NAME,
    SCHEMA_NAME,
    SERVICE_NAME,
    CONSUMPTION_TYPE,
    ROUND(SUM(CREDITS), 4) AS CREDITS
FROM SNOWFLAKE.ACCOUNT_USAGE.CORTEX_SEARCH_DAILY_USAGE_HISTORY
WHERE USAGE_DATE >= DATEADD(DAY, -30, CURRENT_DATE())
GROUP BY 1, 2, 3, 4
ORDER BY CREDITS DESC;

The consumption categories distinguish serving, embedding, and batch usage. When combining this view with AI Functions usage, avoid double-counting embedding credits.

Query 5: Find developers repeatedly running AI functions

First, assign meaningful query tags in your development sessions:

ALTER SESSION SET QUERY_TAG =
  'project=ai_cost_monitor;env=dev;team=data_engineering';

Then investigate the most expensive AI queries alongside query history:

WITH AI_COST AS (
    SELECT
        QUERY_ID,
        SUM(CREDITS) AS AI_CREDITS
    FROM SNOWFLAKE.ACCOUNT_USAGE.CORTEX_AI_FUNCTIONS_USAGE_HISTORY
    WHERE START_TIME >= DATEADD(DAY, -7, CURRENT_TIMESTAMP())
    GROUP BY QUERY_ID
)
SELECT
    Q.USER_NAME,
    Q.QUERY_TAG,
    COUNT(*) AS QUERY_COUNT,
    ROUND(SUM(A.AI_CREDITS), 4) AS AI_CREDITS
FROM AI_COST A
JOIN SNOWFLAKE.ACCOUNT_USAGE.QUERY_HISTORY Q
  ON A.QUERY_ID = Q.QUERY_ID
GROUP BY 1, 2
ORDER BY AI_CREDITS DESC;

This attributes AI-function spending to the SQL user and query tag where query-history records are available. It does not necessarily identify the end user behind a shared service account.

4. Detecting unexpected AI spending

An effective monitoring system should distinguish a normal increase in usage from an abnormal one.

For example, suppose your development environment usually consumes 10 AI credits daily, but suddenly consumes 80.

Illustrative AI credit consumption

Friday’s eightfold increase deserves investigation, but is not automatically evidence of waste.

A simple first step is to compare today’s usage with the previous seven days.

WITH DAILY AS (
    SELECT
        USAGE_DATE,
        SUM(CREDITS_USED) AS CREDITS
    FROM SNOWFLAKE.ACCOUNT_USAGE.METERING_DAILY_HISTORY
    WHERE SERVICE_TYPE = 'AI_FUNCTIONS'
      AND USAGE_DATE >= DATEADD(DAY, -8, CURRENT_DATE())
    GROUP BY 1
),
BASELINE AS (
    SELECT AVG(CREDITS) AS AVG_CREDITS
    FROM DAILY
    WHERE USAGE_DATE BETWEEN
        DATEADD(DAY, -7, CURRENT_DATE())
        AND DATEADD(DAY, -1, CURRENT_DATE())
)
SELECT
    D.USAGE_DATE,
    D.CREDITS,
    B.AVG_CREDITS,
    ROUND(D.CREDITS / NULLIF(B.AVG_CREDITS, 0), 2)
        AS BASELINE_MULTIPLIER
FROM DAILY D
CROSS JOIN BASELINE B
WHERE D.USAGE_DATE = CURRENT_DATE();

This example monitors the AI_FUNCTIONS service type. For a complete AI budget, reconcile all applicable AI service types rather than relying on a single category. Daily metering may also be delayed, so use the appropriate feature-specific views for more timely detection.

5. Unexpected AI costs during development

Development is one of the easiest places to accumulate AI spending without noticing it.

Consider a developer building a product-review classification pipeline.

The initial experiment processes 100 customer reviews. Everything works, so the developer runs the same logic against 100,000 records.

But the SQL query invokes an AI function once per row.

The result is potentially 100,000 model evaluations from a single SQL statement.

Here are common development scenarios that create unexpected costs.

Example: How a simple SQL statement becomes expensive
SELECT
    REVIEW_ID,
    AI_SENTIMENT(REVIEW_TEXT) AS SENTIMENT
FROM CUSTOMER_REVIEWS;

This is straightforward SQL, but processing a large table can generate substantial AI usage.

A safer development approach:

SELECT
    REVIEW_ID,
    AI_SENTIMENT(REVIEW_TEXT) AS SENTIMENT
FROM CUSTOMER_REVIEWS
WHERE REVIEW_TEXT IS NOT NULL
ORDER BY REVIEW_ID
LIMIT 100;

The second query limits the input to 100 records. It is useful for controlled experimentation, although you should not assume that adding LIMIT to every SQL shape guarantees a corresponding reduction in AI evaluations. For expensive workloads, explicitly materialize the sample before invoking AI.

CREATE OR REPLACE TEMP TABLE REVIEW_SAMPLE AS
SELECT REVIEW_ID, REVIEW_TEXT
FROM CUSTOMER_REVIEWS
WHERE REVIEW_TEXT IS NOT NULL
ORDER BY REVIEW_ID
LIMIT 100;
SELECT
    REVIEW_ID,
    AI_SENTIMENT(REVIEW_TEXT) AS SENTIMENT
FROM REVIEW_SAMPLE;

This creates a bounded input dataset before inference begins.

6. A practical cost-control framework

I recommend a five-layer approach.

Snowflake now documents AI-specific resource and shared budgets, as well as per-user quotas for supported features. Budget actions are periodic rather than instantaneous; quotas can block additional requests more quickly.

Suggested development controls

For an organization introducing Snowflake AI, I would start with these policies:

  • Every AI workload must have an identifiable owner and environment.
  • Development AI workloads must have defined credit limits.
  • Production deployments require a cost estimate per 1,000 requests or records.
  • Large-scale AI processing requires an approved input-volume threshold.
  • Repeated inference should use persisted results where appropriate.
  • Agentic applications must have retry and tool-execution limits.
  • Cost anomalies should be investigated before automatic remediation is enabled.

These controls should be applied based on workload criticality. A research experiment and a customer-facing production application should not have identical enforcement rules.

7. Measuring the cost of AI applications

One of the most useful metrics is not simply total credits.

It is cost per successful business outcome.

For example, suppose a document classification application consumes 120 credits to process 40,000 documents, of which 36,000 are successfully classified.

These are illustrative calculations, not observed Snowflake performance.

An optimization that reduces total credits but significantly increases classification errors may actually worsen business economics.

Track inference cost alongside accuracy, latency, retries, and successful outcomes.

8. Implementation roadmap

A practical Snowflake AI FinOps rollout can be organized into four phases.

  1. Week 1 — Visibility: Identify all active AI services, establish daily usage reporting, and classify development versus production consumption.
  2. Week 2 — Attribution: Add query tags, map service accounts to applications, and create project-level cost reporting.
  3. Week 3 — Detection: Establish rolling baselines, unusual-spend alerts, and high-credit query investigations.
  4. Week 4 — Controls: Configure applicable budgets and quotas, implement development guardrails, and test escalation procedures.
Conclusion: AI cost optimization is an engineering discipline

As Snowflake AI adoption grows, cost optimization must extend beyond warehouse sizing and query tuning.

AI workloads introduce new consumption patterns: token processing, document extraction, search serving, multi-step agent execution, and repeated development experimentation.

The most effective approach is to establish visibility first, identify which workloads drive spending, then introduce controls that preserve useful AI capabilities without allowing uncontrolled consumption.

The objective is not to minimize every AI credit. It is to ensure that every AI workload delivers measurable value at a predictable cost.

The question data engineering teams should ask is no longer just, “How much did Snowflake cost?” It is, “Which AI workloads created that cost, why did they consume those resources, and what value did we receive?”

Technical references
  • Snowflake AI cost management and governance
  • Cortex AI Functions usage history
  • Managing Cortex AI Functions costs
  • AI usage and cost attribution reference implementation
