items.title: Building a Production Crowdsourced Data Platform From Scratch
items.summary: Over a few months, I built a crowdsourced data platform from scratch. An 8-Phase Journey through Kubernetes, Kafka, Spark, Airflow, dbt, and Observability on GCP. While working on those phases, I learned much about data concepts and how they are applied in a real-world platform. Photo by JD X on Unsplash What this project is This is a from-scratch clone of a crowdsourced production data engineering stack on GCP, built to learn the real architecture by actually running it: Kafka ingestion, a Spark medallion lake, Airflow orchestration, dbt transformations, a Looker Studio dashboard, Terraform-managed infrastructure, GitHub Actions CI/CD, and full Prometheus/Grafana/Alertmanager observability. A simulator emits fake measurements for 100 mobile devices, representing measurements collected from crowd devices in different locations to build analytical solutions. Those measurements flow through a FastAPI ingest service into Kafka, land in GCS via a sink connector, get progressively refined through a bronze/silver/gold Spark pipeline into BigQuery, get reshaped into analytics-ready marts by dbt, and surface in a Looker Studio dashboard. Airflow orchestrates the whole thing hourly, and Prometheus-based alerting monitors it. In addition, we developed startup/teardown bash scripts to build the required infrastructure between sessions and destroy running resources to control GCP billing costs. The Project Diagram This blog is aimed at data engineers and data scientists who want to know when the real data pipeline actually broke, why, and how we found out. Every phase below includes at least one real debugging story. Several of them took multiple sessions to crack, and two in particular are genuinely instructive about how subtle a wrong assumption can be when the evidence superficially seems to confirm it. Phases 00–01: Terraform foundations and GKE Autopilot Everything starts from a layered Terraform setup, split into modules with different lifecycles: foundations (VPC, NAT, IAM, Workload Identity Federation, service accounts) is long-lived and applied once; gke (the cluster itself, Workload Identity bindings ) is ephemeral and recreated every session; lake and cloudsql sit in between, but separate from the compute layer. The cluster is GKE Autopilot, which trades node management for a set of real constraints you don’t hit on a standard GKE cluster. Each group of Kubernetes pods is isolated in a namespace. Workload Identity is the other piece worth calling out: every pod that needs GCP access (Kafka Connect reading a GCS credential, Spark writing to BigQuery, Airflow workers submitting SparkApplications, dbt reading/writing BigQuery) runs as a Kubernetes ServiceAccount bound to a GCP service account via Workload Identity, never a mounted key file. For example, the same Workload Identity Federation setup lets GitHub Actions authenticate to GCP with zero stored secrets; No service-account JSON key sitting in a GitHub Secret anywhere. Phase 02: Kafka, ingest, and a GCS sink connector Kafka runs via Strimzi in KRaft mode (no ZooKeeper), fronted by a FastAPI ingest service that validates incoming measurements with Pydantic and serializes them to Avro via a Schema Registry before publishing. A GCS Sink Connector then lands the raw Avro files in a landing bucket. The Kafka Connect image itself is a small, instructive lesson in its own right: it’s confluentinc/cp-kafka-connect:7.6.0 plus exactly one layer. confluent-hub install confluentinc/kafka-connect-gcs:10.0.7, but the Dockerfile that built it was never committed anywhere. Months later, reconstructing it required pulling the live image and running docker history; no-trunc against it to recover the exact base image and install command. Lesson for any team running ad-hoc image builds: if the Dockerfile isn’t in version control, the image itself eventually becomes the only source of truth for how it was built, with the image still sitting in a registry. The real debugging story here is the sink connector’s `path.format` configuration. It’s a Joda-Time pattern string (year=YYYY/month=MM/day=dd/hour=HH), and Joda-Time treats every bare letter as a pattern symbol, including the literal characters in words like “year” and “month” themselves. Left unquoted, this throws Illegal pattern component: r at the exact moment the connector’s task tries to start. Critically, this failure happens at the task level, not the connector level. A GET /connectors/ /status call shows the connector itself as RUNNING while its one task sits FAILED, silently. The parent object looks healthy while the actual unit of work underneath it is broken — turned out to be a recurring shape across this whole project, not a one-off. The fix is to quote every literal character: ‘year’=YYYY/’month’=MM/’day’=dd/’hour’=HH. Phase 03: Spark and Data Lake Three Spark jobs implement the classic bronze/silver/gold pattern: bronze_job.py reads raw Avro from landing and writes partitioned Parquet; silver_job.py deduplicates and enriches H3 geohash; gold_job.py aggregates into hourly operator-level metrics and loads them into BigQuery. The one design choice worth flagging to anyone building something similar: every one of these three jobs does a full mode(“overwrite”) of its entire output on every single run. There’s no incremental or delta processing anywhere in this pipeline. bronze_job.py reads everything currently sitting in landing each time it runs, not just what’s new since the last run; gold_job.py truncates and reloads the whole BigQuery table, not just the current hour’s partition. This has a real, concrete operational consequence worth internalizing: a successful job run tells you nothing about data freshness. Early in this project, a bq query returning real-looking rows was mistaken for confirmation that the pipeline was working end-to-end, but it was Spark successfully re-aggregating three-day-old backlog data that had accumulated in landing while a downstream connector was silently broken. The only reliable freshness check is inspecting the actual date values inside the output, not the job’s exit code. Phase 04: Airflow Airflow 2.9.2 runs on KubernetesExecutor, backed by Cloud SQL Postgres, with DAGs synced live from the repo via GitSync. The daily_batch_pipeline DAG chains delete_old_jobs → bronze_job → silver_job → gold_job → dbt_transform, each Spark task submitting a SparkApplication and polling for completion. The defining bug of this phase: a real triggered DAG run had bronze_job fail in well under a second, every single time, while airflow tasks test daily_batch_pipeline bronze_job run manually succeeded fully, submitting and polling a SparkApplication to completion. The difference was invisible until traced carefully: tasks test executes in-process inside the scheduler pod, which runs as the airflow-scheduler ServiceAccount. A real KubernetesExecutor task runs in a separate worker pod, launched with kubernetes_executor.worker_service_account_name, which in this project’s config was a different ServiceAccount (ksa-airflow). The RBAC ClusterRoleBinding granting sparkapplications CRD permissions had only ever been bound to airflow-scheduler — meaning every real task attempt hit an instant 403 Forbidden, while the manual test (running as the already-privileged scheduler identity) worked perfectly and told us nothing was wrong. The general principle: when a manual, in-process reproduction of a task succeeds, but the real scheduled execution fails identically and instantly, suspect an identity mismatch between the two execution contexts before anything else. A task's test success proves the code is correct, not that the deployment’s permissions are. Phase 05: Data transformation (dbt) The dbt project follows a conventional staging/marts split. stg_operator_metrics is a thin view over the raw gold table; daily_operator_summary and operator_rankings are tables built on top of it; bi_operator_daily is a fourth model. A combined view joining the daily summary and the rankings, built specifically so Looker Studio would have one clean source rather than needing to blend two tables in its own UI. The column names year, month, day, hour in the source table read like strings, and the staging model’s first version wrote LPAD(month, 2, ‘0’), which failed immediately with No matching signature for function LPAD: Argument types: INT64, INT64, STRING. The columns were genuinely INT64 in BigQuery, despite looking exactly like the kind of zero-padded string column that naming convention would suggest. The fix was a trivial CAST(month AS STRING) before padding, but it’s a reminder that a column’s name and its apparent values from a cursory SELECT * are not a substitute for checking INFORMATION_SCHEMA or the table’s actual DDL. The operational gotcha worth flagging for anyone running dbt inside Kubernetes rather than a managed dbt Cloud environment: the dbt project is containerized, and the container image is not kept in sync by GitSync. Airflow’s DAG files update live, within about 60 seconds of a push, because GitSync polls the repo directly into the scheduler’s pod. The dbt image does not. A model change requires an explicit Docker build and docker push before the next DAG run will reflect it, something that’s easy to forget once you’re used to everything else in the stack updating itself. Phase 06: Looker Studio The BI layer is deliberately simple: Looker Studio’s native BigQuery connector pointed directly at bi_operator_daily, authenticated via the viewer’s own Google account: no service-account key, no credential file, nothing to rotate. The dashboard focuses on trends over time: download/upload speed and latency as time-series charts broken down by operator, with a date-range control and an operator filter. Looker Studio dashboard for download/upload speeds Worth noting for anyone costing this out: Looker Studio itself is free, including the native BigQuery connector. The only real cost surface is the BigQuery query volume the connector generates on each view/refresh. The cost is negligible here given the table’s size, but worth checking data-source freshness settings on larger projects, since more frequent refreshing means more repeated queries against the same underlying data. Phase 07: CI/CD Pipeline Three GitHub Actions workflows, all authenticated through the Workload Identity Federation pool from Phase 00. No stored service-account keys anywhere in GitHub Secrets. docker-build.yml detects which application changed (ingest-api, simulator, spark, dbt) and rebuilds only that image, tagged with both: latest and the commit SHA. terraform-plan.yml runs fmt/validate/plan per module on every push, read-only. terraform-apply.yml is workflow_dispatch-only — applying real infrastructure changes stays a deliberate, manual action, never automatic. The most instructive failure here: a terraform plan run in CI simply hung for 50 minutes with no output, eventually needing to be cancelled. A required Terraform variable with no default value and no TF_VAR_* environment variable supplying it. Locally, Terraform prompts you interactively for a missing value. On a GitHub Actions runner, there’s no stdin to answer that prompt, so Terraform just sits there, indefinitely, until the job’s hard timeout eventually kills it hours later. Any CI pipeline running Terraform needs -input=false as a baseline default. It converts a silent, multi-hour hang into an immediate, readable error the moment a required value is missing, which is a dramatically better failure mode even though it changes nothing about whether the underlying problem exists. A second, related lesson: cancelling that hung run left an orphaned state lock in the GCS backend (Error acquiring the state lock… conditionNotMet), because killing a CI job mid-flight doesn’t give Terraform a chance to release a lock it had already acquired before getting stuck. terraform force-unlock resolved it, but the general rule is worth stating plainly: any Terraform run that gets killed rather than finishing naturally should be assumed to have left a stale lock behind, and the next attempt should check for that before doing anything else. Phase 08: observability using Prometheus and Grafana The monitoring stack layers three new metric sources onto the existing Prometheus/Grafana/Alertmanager install from Phase 01: a PodMonitor scraping Kafka’s already-configured JMX exporter on the broker pods; a hand-added JMX exporter on Kafka Connect (which, running as a plain Deployment rather than a Strimzi-managed CRD, had no metrics pipeline at all until this phase); and Airflow’s built-in StatsD exporter, customized with extraMappings to turn its dag/task-ID-embedded metric names into real Prometheus labels. Grafana Dashboard On top of the metrics, three PrometheusRules cover Kafka Connect task failure, sustained consumer lag, and Airflow task failure, routed to Slack via Alertmanager, but scoped specifically to alerts carrying a project: data-pipeline label, after an early version that changed the default route accidentally sent every one of the chart’s generic built-in cluster-health alerts (KubeMemoryOvercommit, KubePodNotReady) to the same channel. Alrets landed a Slack channel Conclusion Eight phases, a genuine production-shaped stack, and a working pipeline carrying real (simulated) data from ingestion to a dashboard, with alerting watching over it, built the only way that actually teaches the architecture, which is by running it against a live cluster and letting it break in realistic ways rather than reading about how it’s supposed to work. The full project, including every Terraform module, Kubernetes manifest, Spark job, dbt model, and GitHub Actions workflow referenced above, lives in the project’s repository, with a README covering setup and session-lifecycle details for anyone who wants to run it themselves. GitHub Repository: https://github.com/bassemessam1/crowdsource-data-app-clone Building a Production Crowdsourced Data Platform From Scratch was originally published in Towards AI on Medium, where people are continuing the conversation by highlighting and responding to this story.

There’s no incremental or delta processing anywhere in this pipeline. bronze_job.py reads everything currently sitting in landing each time it runs, not just what’s new since the last run; gold_job.py truncates and reloads the whole BigQuery table, not just the current hour’s partition.

This has a real, concrete operational consequence worth internalizing: a successful job run tells you nothing about data freshness. Early in this project, a bq query returning real-looking rows was mistaken for confirmation that the pipeline was working end-to-end, but it was Spark successfully re-aggregating three-day-old backlog data that had accumulated in landing while a downstream connector was silently broken. The only reliable freshness check is inspecting the actual date values inside the output, not the job’s exit code.

Phase 04: Airflow

Airflow 2.9.2 runs on KubernetesExecutor, backed by Cloud SQL Postgres, with DAGs synced live from the repo via GitSync. The daily_batch_pipeline DAG chains delete_old_jobs → bronze_job → silver_job → gold_job → dbt_transform, each Spark task submitting a SparkApplication and polling for completion.

The defining bug of this phase: a real triggered DAG run had bronze_job fail in well under a second, every single time, while airflow tasks test daily_batch_pipeline bronze_job run manually succeeded fully, submitting and polling a SparkApplication to completion. The difference was invisible until traced carefully: tasks test executes in-process inside the scheduler pod, which runs as the airflow-scheduler ServiceAccount. A real KubernetesExecutor task runs in a separate worker pod, launched with kubernetes_executor.worker_service_account_name, which in this project’s config was a different ServiceAccount (ksa-airflow). The RBAC ClusterRoleBinding granting sparkapplications CRD permissions had only ever been bound to airflow-scheduler — meaning every real task attempt hit an instant 403 Forbidden, while the manual test (running as the already-privileged scheduler identity) worked perfectly and told us nothing was wrong.

The general principle: when a manual, in-process reproduction of a task succeeds, but the real scheduled execution fails identically and instantly, suspect an identity mismatch between the two execution contexts before anything else. A task's test success proves the code is correct, not that the deployment’s permissions are.

Phase 05: Data transformation (dbt)

The dbt project follows a conventional staging/marts split. stg_operator_metrics is a thin view over the raw gold table; daily_operator_summary and operator_rankings are tables built on top of it; bi_operator_daily is a fourth model. A combined view joining the daily summary and the rankings, built specifically so Looker Studio would have one clean source rather than needing to blend two tables in its own UI.

The column names year, month, day, hour in the source table read like strings, and the staging model’s first version wrote LPAD(month, 2, ‘0’), which failed immediately with No matching signature for function LPAD: Argument types: INT64, INT64, STRING. The columns were genuinely INT64 in BigQuery, despite looking exactly like the kind of zero-padded string column that naming convention would suggest. The fix was a trivial CAST(month AS STRING) before padding, but it’s a reminder that a column’s name and its apparent values from a cursory SELECT * are not a substitute for checking INFORMATION_SCHEMA or the table’s actual DDL.

The operational gotcha worth flagging for anyone running dbt inside Kubernetes rather than a managed dbt Cloud environment: the dbt project is containerized, and the container image is not kept in sync by GitSync. Airflow’s DAG files update live, within about 60 seconds of a push, because GitSync polls the repo directly into the scheduler’s pod. The dbt image does not. A model change requires an explicit Docker build and docker push before the next DAG run will reflect it, something that’s easy to forget once you’re used to everything else in the stack updating itself.

Phase 06: Looker Studio

The BI layer is deliberately simple: Looker Studio’s native BigQuery connector pointed directly at bi_operator_daily, authenticated via the viewer’s own Google account: no service-account key, no credential file, nothing to rotate. The dashboard focuses on trends over time: download/upload speed and latency as time-series charts broken down by operator, with a date-range control and an operator filter.

Looker Studio dashboard for download/upload speeds

Worth noting for anyone costing this out: Looker Studio itself is free, including the native BigQuery connector. The only real cost surface is the BigQuery query volume the connector generates on each view/refresh. The cost is negligible here given the table’s size, but worth checking data-source freshness settings on larger projects, since more frequent refreshing means more repeated queries against the same underlying data.

Phase 07: CI/CD Pipeline

Three GitHub Actions workflows, all authenticated through the Workload Identity Federation pool from Phase 00. No stored service-account keys anywhere in GitHub Secrets. docker-build.yml detects which application changed (ingest-api, simulator, spark, dbt) and rebuilds only that image, tagged with both: latest and the commit SHA. terraform-plan.yml runs fmt/validate/plan per module on every push, read-only. terraform-apply.yml is workflow_dispatch-only — applying real infrastructure changes stays a deliberate, manual action, never automatic.

The most instructive failure here: a terraform plan run in CI simply hung for 50 minutes with no output, eventually needing to be cancelled. A required Terraform variable with no default value and no TF_VAR_* environment variable supplying it. Locally, Terraform prompts you interactively for a missing value. On a GitHub Actions runner, there’s no stdin to answer that prompt, so Terraform just sits there, indefinitely, until the job’s hard timeout eventually kills it hours later. Any CI pipeline running Terraform needs -input=false as a baseline default. It converts a silent, multi-hour hang into an immediate, readable error the moment a required value is missing, which is a dramatically better failure mode even though it changes nothing about whether the underlying problem exists.

A second, related lesson: cancelling that hung run left an orphaned state lock in the GCS backend (Error acquiring the state lock… conditionNotMet), because killing a CI job mid-flight doesn’t give Terraform a chance to release a lock it had already acquired before getting stuck. terraform force-unlock resolved it, but the general rule is worth stating plainly: any Terraform run that gets killed rather than finishing naturally should be assumed to have left a stale lock behind, and the next attempt should check for that before doing anything else.

Phase 08: observability using Prometheus and Grafana

The monitoring stack layers three new metric sources onto the existing Prometheus/Grafana/Alertmanager install from Phase 01: a PodMonitor scraping Kafka’s already-configured JMX exporter on the broker pods; a hand-added JMX exporter on Kafka Connect (which, running as a plain Deployment rather than a Strimzi-managed CRD, had no metrics pipeline at all until this phase); and Airflow’s built-in StatsD exporter, customized with extraMappings to turn its dag/task-ID-embedded metric names into real Prometheus labels.

Grafana Dashboard

On top of the metrics, three PrometheusRules cover Kafka Connect task failure, sustained consumer lag, and Airflow task failure, routed to Slack via Alertmanager, but scoped specifically to alerts carrying a project: data-pipeline label, after an early version that changed the default route accidentally sent every one of the chart’s generic built-in cluster-health alerts (KubeMemoryOvercommit, KubePodNotReady) to the same channel.

Alrets landed a Slack channelConclusion

Eight phases, a genuine production-shaped stack, and a working pipeline carrying real (simulated) data from ingestion to a dashboard, with alerting watching over it, built the only way that actually teaches the architecture, which is by running it against a live cluster and letting it break in realistic ways rather than reading about how it’s supposed to work.

The full project, including every Terraform module, Kubernetes manifest, Spark job, dbt model, and GitHub Actions workflow referenced above, lives in the project’s repository, with a README covering setup and session-lifecycle details for anyone who wants to run it themselves.

GitHub Repository:

https://github.com/bassemessam1/crowdsource-data-app-clone

items.title: Open or Closed AI? A Friendly Map of the Four Layers Behind Every AI App
items.summary: Imagine you’ve decided to build an AI chatbot, or maybe a full AI agent. You’re excited. Then the questions hit you all at once. Which model should I use? Where does my data go? How do I wire it all together? Should I use open-source tools, or pay for a managed service? That moment of “where do I even start?” is something almost every builder feels. The good news is that the whole puzzle becomes much easier once you see it as four layers : the model, the data, the orchestration, and the application. At each layer, you can choose open-source or closed, and there’s no single right answer. Let’s walk through it together. Why open source deserves a seat at the table Before the layers, a quick note on why this matters. Researchers at Harvard Business School estimated what it would cost companies to rebuild the open-source software they use from scratch. Their estimate of that demand-side value was $8.8 trillion, and they found firms would need to spend 3.5 times more on software if open source didn’t exist. A fair caution: that number is an estimate built on assumptions, and some experts have questioned how it was calculated. One critic argued the headline figure may be off by an order of magnitude. So think of it less as an exact price tag and more as a sign of how much of the digital world rests on code that people share freely. In AI, that sharing is especially lively. Many features that appear first in commercial tools are soon recreated by the open-source community. One note on scope: this guide covers the software layers only. Hardware and infrastructure matter too, but they’re a separate conversation. Layer 1: The model, the brain of your system The model sits at the center of everything. Here’s how the two paths differ. The open path. You can choose from many open models: general-purpose language models, community fine-tuned versions built for tasks like question answering, or models specialized for a field such as law. There are even narrow tools, like a model that spots anomalies in biomedical images. The catch is that you have to run the model. That means picking an inference engine, the software that actually runs it. For your laptop, a popular option is Ollama. For servers, common choices include vLLM and TensorRT-LLM. The closed path. You call a model through an API. It’s simple, and the rest is handled for you: the inference engine, the speed optimizations, and the infrastructure underneath. You send a request and get an answer. How it feels: closed is like ordering food delivery. Open is like cooking in your own kitchen. One is faster, and the other gives you control over every ingredient. Layer 2: Data, the memory your AI draws from Most useful AI apps need your own information, such as documents, notes, or company knowledge. Here’s something reassuring: this layer looks almost the same for open and closed systems. The pieces are: Data sources and connectors. Automated links that pull information in from your tools. Data conversion. Turning messy material, like a PDF, into structured text an AI can use. RAG pipelines and vector databases. This is where your data is turned into embeddings and stored, so the model can pull the right pieces into its context when needed. What changes is the nature of the tools. With open source, three differences stand out: Cost. Open tools are usually free to use, while closed ones are often part of a paid product. Customization. With the source code in hand, you can adapt it. With closed tools, you work with what’s built in, and if it’s missing, you can’t add it yourself. Control over where it runs. Open code can live on your own servers or any cloud you choose. Closed services are typically hosted for you, so you have less say over where your private data travels. That last point matters a lot if you handle sensitive information. Layer 3: Orchestration, how the work gets organized Orchestration is how your AI system breaks a problem into smaller steps. It can include: Reasoning and planning: deciding how to tackle a task. Executing: calling tools or functions to actually do things. Review loops: checking and improving the answer before it reaches the user. On the open side, this depends on the agent framework you pick, and you control how it’s structured. On the closed side, some commercial platforms let you run agent-style tasks through an API. Here’s the tradeoff, and it’s a fair one. The closed route is simpler, since you just make a call that matches the platform’s format. But sometimes it can be too simple, because you can’t shape the exact structure of your agent the way you can with an open framework. Layer 4: The application, what your users actually touch This is the part people see: the chat window, the buttons, the experience. On the open side, there are two flavors: Customization-first: tools like Open WebUI and AnythingLLM give you full control over the user experience. Speed-first: tools like Gradio and Streamlit let you build a web interface in minutes with minimal setup. On the closed side, the usual route is to build from scratch, embedding the AI directly into your web or mobile app. The four layers at a glance Layer Open-source path Closed path Model Run it yourself with Ollama, vLLM, or TensorRT-LLM Call an API; inference is managed for you Data Connectors, conversion, RAG, and vector DBs: free, customizable, deployable anywhere Same building blocks, but part of paid products with less control Orchestration Choose an agent framework and control the structure Platform APIs; simpler, but less flexible Application Open WebUI, AnythingLLM, Gradio, Streamlit Build the interface inside your own app A few honest things to keep in mind I love the freedom open source offers, but I’d be doing you a disservice if I only talked about the upside. “Free” isn’t always cheap. The software may cost nothing, but running models takes hardware, time, and know-how. More control means more responsibility. Updates, security, and reliability become your job. “Open” can mean different things. Some models share their weights but have restrictive licenses. Always read the license before building a product on it. Tools change fast. This landscape moves quickly, so check each project’s current documentation before you commit. How to choose, without the stress You don’t have to go all open or all closed. Many good systems mix both. A few questions can guide you: How sensitive is my data? If privacy and location matter, open and self-hosted options give you more control. How fast do I need to launch? For a quick start, closed APIs and tools like Gradio or Streamlit save time. Do I need to customize deeply? If yes, open source gives you room to adapt. What can my team maintain? Be honest about your time and skills. What will it cost at scale? Compare API fees with running your own setup. If you’re just beginning, here’s a gentle path: try a small open model on your laptop with Ollama, build a simple interface with Gradio or Streamlit, and see how it feels. You’ll learn more in an afternoon than in a week of reading. Understanding these four layers, model, data, orchestration, and application, turns a confusing pile of choices into something you can reason about. Sometimes the convenience of a closed solution is exactly right. Other times, the transparency and flexibility of open source will serve you better. Either way, it’s worth remembering that the open option exists, shaped by a community that keeps building and sharing. That’s a hopeful thing to build on. Open or Closed AI? A Friendly Map of the Four Layers Behind Every AI App was originally published in Towards AI on Medium, where people are continuing the conversation by highlighting and responding to this story.
items.summary_html:
Imagine you’ve decided to build an AI chatbot, or maybe a full AI agent. You’re excited. Then the questions hit you all at once. Which model should I use? Where does my data go? How do I wire it all together? Should I use open-source tools, or pay for a managed service?

That moment of “where do I even start?” is something almost every builder feels. The good news is that the whole puzzle becomes much easier once you see it as four layers: the model, the data, the orchestration, and the application. At each layer, you can choose open-source or closed, and there’s no single right answer.

Let’s walk through it together.

Why open source deserves a seat at the table

Before the layers, a quick note on why this matters. Researchers at Harvard Business School estimated what it would cost companies to rebuild the open-source software they use from scratch. Their estimate of that demand-side value was $8.8 trillion, and they found firms would need to spend 3.5 times more on software if open source didn’t exist.

A fair caution: that number is an estimate built on assumptions, and some experts have questioned how it was calculated. One critic argued the headline figure may be off by an order of magnitude. So think of it less as an exact price tag and more as a sign of how much of the digital world rests on code that people share freely.

In AI, that sharing is especially lively. Many features that appear first in commercial tools are soon recreated by the open-source community.

One note on scope: this guide covers the software layers only. Hardware and infrastructure matter too, but they’re a separate conversation.

Layer 1: The model, the brain of your system

The model sits at the center of everything. Here’s how the two paths differ.

The open path. You can choose from many open models: general-purpose language models, community fine-tuned versions built for tasks like question answering, or models specialized for a field such as law. There are even narrow tools, like a model that spots anomalies in biomedical images.

The catch is that you have to run the model. That means picking an inference engine, the software that actually runs it. For your laptop, a popular option is Ollama. For servers, common choices include vLLM and TensorRT-LLM.

The closed path. You call a model through an API. It’s simple, and the rest is handled for you: the inference engine, the speed optimizations, and the infrastructure underneath. You send a request and get an answer.

How it feels: closed is like ordering food delivery. Open is like cooking in your own kitchen. One is faster, and the other gives you control over every ingredient.

Layer 2: Data, the memory your AI draws from

Most useful AI apps need your own information, such as documents, notes, or company knowledge. Here’s something reassuring: this layer looks almost the same for open and closed systems. The pieces are:

  1. Data sources and connectors. Automated links that pull information in from your tools.
  2. Data conversion. Turning messy material, like a PDF, into structured text an AI can use.
  3. RAG pipelines and vector databases. This is where your data is turned into embeddings and stored, so the model can pull the right pieces into its context when needed.

What changes is the nature of the tools. With open source, three differences stand out:

  • Cost. Open tools are usually free to use, while closed ones are often part of a paid product.
  • Customization. With the source code in hand, you can adapt it. With closed tools, you work with what’s built in, and if it’s missing, you can’t add it yourself.
  • Control over where it runs. Open code can live on your own servers or any cloud you choose. Closed services are typically hosted for you, so you have less say over where your private data travels.

That last point matters a lot if you handle sensitive information.

Layer 3: Orchestration, how the work gets organized

Orchestration is how your AI system breaks a problem into smaller steps. It can include:

  • Reasoning and planning: deciding how to tackle a task.
  • Executing: calling tools or functions to actually do things.
  • Review loops: checking and improving the answer before it reaches the user.

On the open side, this depends on the agent framework you pick, and you control how it’s structured. On the closed side, some commercial platforms let you run agent-style tasks through an API.

Here’s the tradeoff, and it’s a fair one. The closed route is simpler, since you just make a call that matches the platform’s format. But sometimes it can be too simple, because you can’t shape the exact structure of your agent the way you can with an open framework.

Layer 4: The application, what your users actually touch

This is the part people see: the chat window, the buttons, the experience.

On the open side, there are two flavors:

  • Customization-first: tools like Open WebUI and AnythingLLM give you full control over the user experience.
  • Speed-first: tools like Gradio and Streamlit let you build a web interface in minutes with minimal setup.

On the closed side, the usual route is to build from scratch, embedding the AI directly into your web or mobile app.

The four layers at a glance

Layer Open-source path Closed path Model Run it yourself with Ollama, vLLM, or TensorRT-LLM Call an API; inference is managed for you Data Connectors, conversion, RAG, and vector DBs: free, customizable, deployable anywhere Same building blocks, but part of paid products with less control Orchestration Choose an agent framework and control the structure Platform APIs; simpler, but less flexible Application Open WebUI, AnythingLLM, Gradio, Streamlit Build the interface inside your own app

A few honest things to keep in mind

I love the freedom open source offers, but I’d be doing you a disservice if I only talked about the upside.

  • “Free” isn’t always cheap. The software may cost nothing, but running models takes hardware, time, and know-how.
  • More control means more responsibility. Updates, security, and reliability become your job.
  • “Open” can mean different things. Some models share their weights but have restrictive licenses. Always read the license before building a product on it.
  • Tools change fast. This landscape moves quickly, so check each project’s current documentation before you commit.
How to choose, without the stress

You don’t have to go all open or all closed. Many good systems mix both. A few questions can guide you:

  1. How sensitive is my data? If privacy and location matter, open and self-hosted options give you more control.
  2. How fast do I need to launch? For a quick start, closed APIs and tools like Gradio or Streamlit save time.
  3. Do I need to customize deeply? If yes, open source gives you room to adapt.
  4. What can my team maintain? Be honest about your time and skills.
  5. What will it cost at scale? Compare API fees with running your own setup.

If you’re just beginning, here’s a gentle path: try a small open model on your laptop with Ollama, build a simple interface with Gradio or Streamlit, and see how it feels. You’ll learn more in an afternoon than in a week of reading.

Understanding these four layers, model, data, orchestration, and application, turns a confusing pile of choices into something you can reason about. Sometimes the convenience of a closed solution is exactly right. Other times, the transparency and flexibility of open source will serve you better.

Either way, it’s worth remembering that the open option exists, shaped by a community that keeps building and sharing. That’s a hopeful thing to build on.

items.title: Beyond Faster Development: How AI Is Reshaping Product, Engineering, QA and Delivery Workflows
items.summary: AI is changing product development as well as collaboration and delivery within teams. Product development consisted of well-defined steps: figuring out what to build, designing solutions, creating prototypes, testing, and scaling up, which required human effort. With the introduction of AI, many software development steps have been automated, making development much faster. Coding, testing, and deployment shaped how teams worked. Product managers collected requirements, engineers implemented them, and QA checked everything according to processes designed to minimize handoff delays. Nowadays, AI is making many parts of software development faster, from prototyping and coding to testing and delivery. But faster development does not mean better results. Teams can build faster and still build features users don’t need, miss important risks, or spend more time reviewing and reworking changes. The shift should be from faster development to solving business problems. The question should be: Are we solving the right problem? Does our solution fit? Has our solution helped users? That shift affects each team differently, but they must ensure they solve the right problem and deliver something valuable. Product: deciding what’s worth building Product management must allocate engineering resources efficiently, since product development is costly. In Agile and similar frameworks, product managers research business needs, engage with users, collect and document feedback, review it with stakeholders, and consult engineers. Because each step takes significant time and effort, teams must define priorities and decide what to build before development starts. AI can reduce development costs by automating some steps, giving teams more time to think creatively and make decisions. Instead of extensive PRDs, teams can create prototypes and get feedback quickly. Today, product managers and designers use AI to turn ideas into interactive, testable prototypes, speeding up discovery. This approach is especially useful during discovery. A prototype can help answer questions like these: Do users understand the workflow? Is the proposed interaction confusing? Does the concept solve the problem we think it solves? Which assumptions require further investigation? Prototypes can help with decisions, but they do not guarantee product-market fit. Beyond prototyping, product teams can use AI to summarize customer interviews, cluster support tickets into themes, draft user stories and acceptance criteria, query usage data, and draft release notes. AI prepares the material; the product manager validates it and makes the call. The main challenges are building features users don’t need, AI summaries that miss nuance, and pressure to ship prototypes. Product teams should remember these principles: Preserve fundamentals: Understand customers and properly frame the problem. Use AI to gain a broad perspective, but validate its insights against real evidence. Use prototypes to learn, not to ship. A compelling prototype is not a production-ready system. Design features with possible failures in mind. Show uncertainty, explain your recommendations, and make it easy to correct mistakes. Proper boundaries help to build trust. Monitor and verify output of AI with product metrics. Define success metrics before building to avoid features users don’t need. Strategy, tradeoffs between revenue, experience, and risk, and the definition of success still belong to people. Engineering: the bottleneck is context, not code Software engineering is more than coding. The proper architecture, integration, and reliability rely on system understanding and past decisions. New engineers learn through implementation, debugging, and collaboration. AI can speed up coding, especially for repetitive, well-defined tasks. AI can help engineers understand unfamiliar modules, explore various architectures, debug code, and perform code reviews. However, the key isn’t speed; it’s how engineers use context as AI changes handoffs and reviews. But productivity improvements are not consistent. In early 2025, a METR study found that experienced developers took 19% longer with AI tools, even though they believed they were working faster. METR’s 2026 follow-up suggests newer tools likely speed developers up, but the size of the gain is hard to measure reliably. When requirements are clear and project-specific guidance exists, AI can do more than generate code. Spec-driven development leads to predictable outcomes. AI-generated code is hard to check because it often lacks unwritten requirements or business logic. Without clear guidance, engineers may act on the wrong assumptions. Code review is more demanding. Reviewing individual lines is insufficient when changes span modules, affect shared data, or introduce architectural trade-offs. Reviewers must ensure the implementation meets original requirements and preserves critical system invariants As AI takes over routine tasks, junior engineers may lose opportunities to build system understanding and judgment. The team can address it by deliberately expanding junior engineers responsibilities by providing them training to conduct code reviews, write strict and detailed specifications. The main challenges are review overload, AI-suggested vulnerable dependencies, and overestimated productivity gains. The following practices can be particularly helpful for the engineering teams: Use the specification-driven development techniques, i.e. explicitly define requirements, acceptance criteria, and examples of behavior before implementing the feature. Document architectural decisions, key invariants, and project conventions to give AI tools with a proper context. Treat code reviews as a gate of quality. Adjust review depth based on risk, and make sure the reviewer understands what they are reviewing. Leverage AI to implement and review changes, but keep the ownership and decisions with engineers. Keep hands-on problem-solving and mentorship to develop long-term engineering judgment. Measure reviews, reworks, defects, and maintainability, and security risks but not coding productivity. Security evaluation should include vulnerable dependencies, insecure coding patterns, and hallucinated or unverified code. AI can reduce coding effort, but reliable engineering depends on clear specs, solid reviews, and sound judgment. QA: more tests aren’t the same as better validation Traditionally, QA was the final checkpoint before release. QA teams were measured by the number of test cases and defects they found. Many teams now start testing earlier, with developers writing unit tests and QA joining planning. However, the core question remains the same: proving that software does what it has to. AI can generate test cases from the requirements and code, suggest edge and negative scenarios, automate tests, analyze failures, detect patterns in large test suites, and help QA teams explore additional scenarios. With AI QA teams spend less time on repetitive tests and devote more time to critical validation. However, faster test generation does not mean better validation. When AI generates code and tests from the same requirement, it can make similar mistakes in both. If the requirement is unclear, both AI and humans may make similar mistakes, and bugs can be missed. Thus, analyzing the requirements becomes crucial for QA teams. They should go beyond test results and evaluate if tests actually validate the right risks, use the right data, and cover all scenarios. Tests for AI-generated features can be hard to validate because they may change over time. QA teams usually need to go beyond the regression suite. The main challenges are bloated test suites, false confidence from coverage numbers, and non-deterministic AI features The following changes will help QA teams adjust their processes to the new situation: Define quality standards before generating tests : Define acceptance criteria, key user journeys, failure points, and risk levels early in the process. Use specification-driven testing : Convert requirements and examples into actions and only then allow AI to generate code and tests. Focus on quality, not on quantity. Eliminate duplicates and ensure tests cover edge cases, negative cases, integrations, permissions, and state dependencies. Align testing strategy with risk level: Use unit tests for well-defined rules, integration tests for interactions, end-to-end tests for the key user journeys, and exploratory testing to discover issues that you did not anticipate. Use realistic data during testing. Tests are useless for validating business rules if they don’t replicate the state when the rule applies. Validate AI-powered features: Do this with evaluation sets and acceptance thresholds, since their outputs can vary for the same input. Improve continuously: Create the feedback loop by using production incidents, near-misses, and user actions to create new tests, evaluations, and monitoring alerts. AI helps QA teams automate testing, but QA remains responsible for deciding what evidence is enough to believe the product is ready for release. The goal is strong evidence, not just more tests. Delivery: measuring the right thing Delivery focused on measuring plans against dates. Teams relied on stand-up status updates, spreadsheets, story points, velocities, and closed tickets. Even with DORA metrics such as lead time and change failure rate, cross-team dependencies and decision delays became obvious only after affecting the schedule. AI can help teams become more productive. Product teams can create prototypes faster, engineering teams can implement faster, and QA teams can generate more test cases. The data necessary to understand delivery flow always existed in tickets, pull requests, reviews, builds, deployments, and incidents. Now, AI helps to link all these pieces of data to figure out where work is delayed, whether due to coding, decision wait time, dependency wait time, or late defects. This creates a more holistic view of delivery rather than treating each team’s output as a separate measure of progress. Higher output is often mistaken for higher productivity. Teams can increase the volume of pull requests, but this does not necessarily reduce the time to release for customers. What is important is the flow from development to customer outcome. To accurately assess delivery performance and drive meaningful improvements, teams can adopt key practices across these core areas: Measure output and outcomes: Use metrics such as lead time, decision wait time, dependency wait time, change failure rate, defects escaped, adoption rate, reliability, and customer behavior. Waiting time visibility: Make waiting times visible by tracking how long work is blocked by decisions, approvals, dependencies, or missing context. Address the processes causing these delays. Measure the entire flow: Compare coding speed with the review, rework, release, and operation times to avoid the illusion of improvements in one stage only. Create a shared view across teams: Connect data across teams to provide Product, Engineering, and QA with a shared understanding of where work is slowing down, the context is lost, and dependencies are created. AI to analyze flow: Use AI to analyze the flow, but not to generate status reports. Let AI identify bottlenecks, summarize delivery patterns, and assist with forecasting, but don’t delegate interpreting and acting on this data to AI. Engineering productivity is measured by how efficiently decisions turn into customer outcomes. What stays human Accountability questions may arise as AI becomes more involved, but people remain responsible for the outcomes. What remains uniquely human is not performing every task,but making the decisions that involve context and judgment. items.summary_html:
AI is changing product development as well as collaboration and delivery within teams. Product development consisted of well-defined steps: figuring out what to build, designing solutions, creating prototypes, testing, and scaling up, which required human effort. With the introduction of AI, many software development steps have been automated, making development much faster.

Coding, testing, and deployment shaped how teams worked. Product managers collected requirements, engineers implemented them, and QA checked everything according to processes designed to minimize handoff delays.

Nowadays, AI is making many parts of software development faster, from prototyping and coding to testing and delivery. But faster development does not mean better results.

Teams can build faster and still build features users don’t need, miss important risks, or spend more time reviewing and reworking changes.

The shift should be from faster development to solving business problems. The question should be: Are we solving the right problem? Does our solution fit? Has our solution helped users?

That shift affects each team differently, but they must ensure they solve the right problem and deliver something valuable.

Product: deciding what’s worth building

Product management must allocate engineering resources efficiently, since product development is costly. In Agile and similar frameworks, product managers research business needs, engage with users, collect and document feedback, review it with stakeholders, and consult engineers. Because each step takes significant time and effort, teams must define priorities and decide what to build before development starts.

AI can reduce development costs by automating some steps, giving teams more time to think creatively and make decisions. Instead of extensive PRDs, teams can create prototypes and get feedback quickly. Today, product managers and designers use AI to turn ideas into interactive, testable prototypes, speeding up discovery.

This approach is especially useful during discovery. A prototype can help answer questions like these:

  • Do users understand the workflow?
  • Is the proposed interaction confusing?
  • Does the concept solve the problem we think it solves?
  • Which assumptions require further investigation?

Prototypes can help with decisions, but they do not guarantee product-market fit.

Beyond prototyping, product teams can use AI to summarize customer interviews, cluster support tickets into themes, draft user stories and acceptance criteria, query usage data, and draft release notes. AI prepares the material; the product manager validates it and makes the call.

The main challenges are building features users don’t need, AI summaries that miss nuance, and pressure to ship prototypes.

Product teams should remember these principles:

  • Preserve fundamentals: Understand customers and properly frame the problem.
  • Use AI to gain a broad perspective, but validate its insights against real evidence.
  • Use prototypes to learn, not to ship. A compelling prototype is not a production-ready system.
  • Design features with possible failures in mind. Show uncertainty, explain your recommendations, and make it easy to correct mistakes. Proper boundaries help to build trust.
  • Monitor and verify output of AI with product metrics.
  • Define success metrics before building to avoid features users don’t need.

Strategy, tradeoffs between revenue, experience, and risk, and the definition of success still belong to people.

Engineering: the bottleneck is context, not code

Software engineering is more than coding. The proper architecture, integration, and reliability rely on system understanding and past decisions. New engineers learn through implementation, debugging, and collaboration.

AI can speed up coding, especially for repetitive, well-defined tasks. AI can help engineers understand unfamiliar modules, explore various architectures, debug code, and perform code reviews. However, the key isn’t speed; it’s how engineers use context as AI changes handoffs and reviews.

But productivity improvements are not consistent. In early 2025, a METR study found that experienced developers took 19% longer with AI tools, even though they believed they were working faster. METR’s 2026 follow-up suggests newer tools likely speed developers up, but the size of the gain is hard to measure reliably.

When requirements are clear and project-specific guidance exists, AI can do more than generate code. Spec-driven development leads to predictable outcomes.

AI-generated code is hard to check because it often lacks unwritten requirements or business logic. Without clear guidance, engineers may act on the wrong assumptions.

Code review is more demanding. Reviewing individual lines is insufficient when changes span modules, affect shared data, or introduce architectural trade-offs. Reviewers must ensure the implementation meets original requirements and preserves critical system invariants

As AI takes over routine tasks, junior engineers may lose opportunities to build system understanding and judgment. The team can address it by deliberately expanding junior engineers responsibilities by providing them training to conduct code reviews, write strict and detailed specifications.

The main challenges are review overload, AI-suggested vulnerable dependencies, and overestimated productivity gains.

The following practices can be particularly helpful for the engineering teams:

  • Use the specification-driven development techniques, i.e. explicitly define requirements, acceptance criteria, and examples of behavior before implementing the feature.
  • Document architectural decisions, key invariants, and project conventions to give AI tools with a proper context.
  • Treat code reviews as a gate of quality. Adjust review depth based on risk, and make sure the reviewer understands what they are reviewing.
  • Leverage AI to implement and review changes, but keep the ownership and decisions with engineers.
  • Keep hands-on problem-solving and mentorship to develop long-term engineering judgment.
  • Measure reviews, reworks, defects, and maintainability, and security risks but not coding productivity. Security evaluation should include vulnerable dependencies, insecure coding patterns, and hallucinated or unverified code.

AI can reduce coding effort, but reliable engineering depends on clear specs, solid reviews, and sound judgment.

QA: more tests aren’t the same as better validation

Traditionally, QA was the final checkpoint before release. QA teams were measured by the number of test cases and defects they found.

Many teams now start testing earlier, with developers writing unit tests and QA joining planning. However, the core question remains the same: proving that software does what it has to.

AI can generate test cases from the requirements and code, suggest edge and negative scenarios, automate tests, analyze failures, detect patterns in large test suites, and help QA teams explore additional scenarios.

With AI QA teams spend less time on repetitive tests and devote more time to critical validation. However, faster test generation does not mean better validation.

When AI generates code and tests from the same requirement, it can make similar mistakes in both. If the requirement is unclear, both AI and humans may make similar mistakes, and bugs can be missed.

Thus, analyzing the requirements becomes crucial for QA teams. They should go beyond test results and evaluate if tests actually validate the right risks, use the right data, and cover all scenarios.

Tests for AI-generated features can be hard to validate because they may change over time. QA teams usually need to go beyond the regression suite.

The main challenges are bloated test suites, false confidence from coverage numbers, and non-deterministic AI features

The following changes will help QA teams adjust their processes to the new situation:

  • Define quality standards before generating tests: Define acceptance criteria, key user journeys, failure points, and risk levels early in the process.
  • Use specification-driven testing: Convert requirements and examples into actions and only then allow AI to generate code and tests. Focus on quality, not on quantity. Eliminate duplicates and ensure tests cover edge cases, negative cases, integrations, permissions, and state dependencies.
  • Align testing strategy with risk level: Use unit tests for well-defined rules, integration tests for interactions, end-to-end tests for the key user journeys, and exploratory testing to discover issues that you did not anticipate. Use realistic data during testing. Tests are useless for validating business rules if they don’t replicate the state when the rule applies.
  • Validate AI-powered features: Do this with evaluation sets and acceptance thresholds, since their outputs can vary for the same input.
  • Improve continuously: Create the feedback loop by using production incidents, near-misses, and user actions to create new tests, evaluations, and monitoring alerts.

AI helps QA teams automate testing, but QA remains responsible for deciding what evidence is enough to believe the product is ready for release. The goal is strong evidence, not just more tests.

Delivery: measuring the right thing

Delivery focused on measuring plans against dates. Teams relied on stand-up status updates, spreadsheets, story points, velocities, and closed tickets. Even with DORA metrics such as lead time and change failure rate, cross-team dependencies and decision delays became obvious only after affecting the schedule.

AI can help teams become more productive. Product teams can create prototypes faster, engineering teams can implement faster, and QA teams can generate more test cases. The data necessary to understand delivery flow always existed in tickets, pull requests, reviews, builds, deployments, and incidents. Now, AI helps to link all these pieces of data to figure out where work is delayed, whether due to coding, decision wait time, dependency wait time, or late defects.

This creates a more holistic view of delivery rather than treating each team’s output as a separate measure of progress.

Higher output is often mistaken for higher productivity. Teams can increase the volume of pull requests, but this does not necessarily reduce the time to release for customers. What is important is the flow from development to customer outcome.

To accurately assess delivery performance and drive meaningful improvements, teams can adopt key practices across these core areas:

  • Measure output and outcomes: Use metrics such as lead time, decision wait time, dependency wait time, change failure rate, defects escaped, adoption rate, reliability, and customer behavior.
  • Waiting time visibility: Make waiting times visible by tracking how long work is blocked by decisions, approvals, dependencies, or missing context. Address the processes causing these delays.
  • Measure the entire flow: Compare coding speed with the review, rework, release, and operation times to avoid the illusion of improvements in one stage only.
  • Create a shared view across teams: Connect data across teams to provide Product, Engineering, and QA with a shared understanding of where work is slowing down, the context is lost, and dependencies are created.
  • AI to analyze flow: Use AI to analyze the flow, but not to generate status reports. Let AI identify bottlenecks, summarize delivery patterns, and assist with forecasting, but don’t delegate interpreting and acting on this data to AI.

Engineering productivity is measured by how efficiently decisions turn into customer outcomes.

What stays human

Accountability questions may arise as AI becomes more involved, but people remain responsible for the outcomes.

What remains uniquely human is not performing every task,but making the decisions that involve context and judgment.

  • Purpose: deciding what problem is worth solving, for whom, and how to measure success.
  • Context: understanding business constraints, system history, past failures, and why certain rules exist.
  • Trade-offs: making decisions on speed vs risk, changing architecture, or rejecting proposed shortcuts.
  • Validation: defining what evidence is enough to believe in the release and that the system behaves correctly in conditions that matter.
  • Ownership: having the single person or the team that is responsible for the decision and its outcomes if something goes wrong.

These responsibilities should not shift between teams.Product, Engineering, QA, and Delivery teams work together continuously in this cycle: the Product team defines the problem and success criteria, engineering teams design and implement the solution,QA teams assess the behavior and risks,delivery teams release the product, measure the results, and feed the feedback into future decisions.

AI supports this process by providing shared context. It connects customer feedback, requirements, code changes, test results, production data, and delivery data. AI can summarize, compare, generate, and highlight patterns. However, it only provides information to support decisions, not make them.

The distinction is whether the work is low-risk and reversible or it affects finance, permissions, sensitive data, key workflows, or customer outcomes. The greater the impact, the more human review, evidence, and ownership are required.

From faster development to better outcomes

AI has the greatest impact on software teams when it transforms collaborative decision-making. Speeding up code development is only one aspect. Product can prototype faster, Engineering can deliver faster, QA can validate more, and Delivery can analyze more data. However, none of these improvements can happen if teams are slow to resolve ambiguities, review changes, validate results, and learn from production outcomes.

This isn’t about competing with AI on productivity. AI should handle repetitive tasks, but people should focus on work that requires context, judgment, and responsibility.

As software development becomes easier, the major challenge becomes defining what is worth building and proving its effectiveness.

items.title: Claude Code Mods Explained: What They Can Do That Hooks and Skills Can’t
items.summary: I built one to find the edges. How mods work, what they can reach, and the bugs that taught me the most. “All tests pass.” Claude Code said it at the end of a long turn, and the run was green. In the same turn, it had also edited tests/conftest.py. Nothing in the transcript hid that. It sat on line 31 of 33 lines of reads, edits and test logs. I scroll past line 31 on most days. So when Anthropic shipped mods in Claude Code, the first thing I built was a mod that puts that line where I can’t miss it. This article is what I learned about mods while doing it: what they are, how the pieces fit, what a mod can reach on your machine, and the bugs that taught me the most. Image by the author. What a mod is A mod is a Claude Code plugin that changes how Claude Code looks and behaves. It is a JavaScript or TypeScript file of event handlers. Claude Code calls a handler when something happens: a tool call, a submitted prompt, a part of the screen about to be drawn. The handler can watch the event, change it, or take it over. Mods arrived in Claude Code 2.1.287. They run in the terminal CLI, the Code tab of the Desktop app and the VS Code extension. You need no Node.js, bundler or build step: Claude Code loads the .ts file directly. Mods vs settings hooks, skills and MCP servers Claude Code already had ways to extend it, so the first question is when a mod is the right tool. The short answer: settings hooks, skills, status lines and MCP servers work from outside Claude Code. A mod runs inside it. Settings hook: a shell command, HTTP call or prompt from a settings file. Good for blocking or logging a tool call, or running a formatter. Skill: text Claude reads. Good for teaching Claude a workflow. MCP server: a separate process. Good for giving Claude new tools and data. Mod: functions inside Claude Code. Good for drawing UI, redrawing Claude Code’s own UI, and stepping into a call or a request. Being inside buys you five things the others can’t do: Draw an interface: a pane beside the transcript or a band above the prompt, with tabs, buttons and text fields. Redraw Claude Code’s own interface: replace a tool call’s row, the spinner, or the question dialog. Step into a tool call or a model request: hold a call while you ask the user, answer it without running the tool, or send one request to a different model. Run code on a command: a /command that runs your function at once, with no Claude turn, even while Claude works. Share data between hooks: one hook counts tool calls, another shows the count beside the spinner. If a settings hook already does the job, use the settings hook. I needed number 2, so a mod was the only option. The three parts: events, render sites and $ Everything in a mod is one of three things. Events decide when your code runs. The ones I used most follow a turn, which is everything Claude does to answer one prompt: turn.start fires when a turn begins and gives you a turnId. turn.step fires before each request to the model. A turn with tool calls has several. turn.complete fires when the turn ends, including one you interrupted. It carries the answer, the duration and the token usage. Return { text } and Claude Code shows a line under the answer. tool.call fires for each tool call. You can pass it on, change it or refuse it. Render sites are the places in the screen you can draw. A ui.render hook fires each time Claude Code is about to draw one, and you pick the site with a matcher such as { component: 'Spinner' }. Sites include ToolUse, ToolGroup, AssistantMessage, Spinner, TurnDuration, PromptHint, AbovePrompt (the band above the prompt) and Pane. Each site gets e.surface, which says whether the terminal, Desktop or VS Code is drawing. $ is the mods API. Every hook gets it as its first argument. Its methods sit in namespaces: $.ui (open panes, notify, set the status line), $.session (messages, usage, the project root), $.store (a key-value store every session on the machine shares), $.clock, $.fs, $.process, $.http, $.model and more. Here is a whole mod in that shape. It adds a line under each answer with the time and the share of context used: import type { Register } from 'claude-code' export const register: Register = (on) => { on('turn.complete', async ($, e, next) => { const r = await next(e) if (e.agentId !== undefined) return r // skip subagent turns const { context } = await $.session.usage() const secs = Math.round(e.durationMs / 1000) return { text: `${secs}s · context ${context.percent}% full` } }) } Two habits from that example carry over to every mod. Call next(e) so the mods after yours still run. And check e.agentId, because subagent turns fire the same events. The build loop You can ask Claude to write a mod: describe it in a session, and Claude writes the plugin. To work on one yourself, three commands do most of the work: claude --plugin-dir . # run Claude Code with your mod; a save reloads it claude plugin validate . # check the manifest and list every hook and call claude plugin test . # run the mod's tests The reload on save is what makes mods fast to build. I change a render hook, save, and the row redraws in the session I already have open. Anthropic also shares three sample mods in its claude-code-playground repository: token-weather (a forecast of your context window above the prompt), blast-radius (holds a risky command such as rm -rf and shows what it would change) and replay-theater (a /replay command that steps through the last turn's edits). Read them before you write your first one. What a mod can reach This part matters more than the API. A mod is not sandboxed. Once it loads, it runs with your permissions. It can read and write your files, start programs, make network requests, read your environment variables, see every prompt and tool call, and approve a tool call before you are asked. Turning on Claude Code’s sandbox does not cover it: the sandbox wraps the Bash commands Claude runs, not processes a mod starts. So before you install a mod, read what it does. Clone it and run claude plugin validate on the folder. The hooks: and calls: lines list every event it handles and every API it calls, without running it. A mod that only draws rows should not list $.http.fetch or $.process.run. If you want to stop all mods, claude --safe-mode turns them off for one session, and "disableAllHooks": true in ~/.claude/settings.json turns them off everywhere. A worked example: TL;DR for Claude Code The mod I built is TL;DR for Claude Code. It folds each turn into one row in Claude Code’s own style: the files Claude changed, the tests before and after, and what to check before you trust the result. Every raw line stays one click away. It is free and open source (MIT), and I’m the only author. Here is how it maps onto the three parts: Events: tool.call reads each call and its result, then passes it on unchanged. turn.start and turn.complete open and close the row. session.compact keeps rows when you run /compact. Render sites: ToolUse and ToolGroup draw the row in place of the tool rows. Spinner names the current job, such as Reading src/auth.py. AbovePrompt draws a context bar. Three Panes hold the detail, the context and the history. $: $.store keeps finished rows (50 per session) and how long each command took last time. $.session.usage feeds the context bar. $.ui.notify pings you when a turn over 30 seconds ends. The calls it does not make are the point. It makes no $.http or $.model calls and starts no processes. It reads everything from what Claude Code reports. The row flags the edits that can fake a green run: Image by the author. What I learned building it 1. A static reader misses more than you expect TL;DR reads each Bash command as text. It never runs or expands a command to learn what it did. I chose that for privacy and safety. The cost showed up fast. I wrote 30 edge cases, and the first version missed many: quoted paths, sudo tee, a cd before a write, mv into a folder, git restore, find -delete, and echo "npm test", which it counted as a test run. Then a live turn wrote a script with S=/tmp/x.sh; cat > "$S" and the row showed nothing. Now the reader follows variables the command sets. My rule became: name what the text names, and drop what it can't name. A path built from $OUT drops out, because a row that says $OUT via Bash reads like a real file name. 2. A wrapper can hide a failure I run a hook that wraps test output and prints its own summary line, such as Go test: 20 passed, 2 failed. The first parser didn't know that line. A failing run showed green. Pipes do the same: in go test | tail, the exit code is tail's. Now a failure in the output counts as a failure, whatever the exit code says. If your mod reports test results, test it against the wrappers you actually use. 3. Real data breaks your layout A flag once quoted a whole heredoc command. The check line was 6,000 characters. Now each flag is one line, cut at the row’s edge, and it names the act, not the command: force push, skipped hooks. The commands behind it open in a pane. 4. Deleting made it look native The first version was a seven-row box with labels, buttons, a diff pane and hint lines. On a dark terminal the labels were almost invisible, and a 60-file refactor took nine rows of cut-off file names. Version 0.1.5 removed the box, the buttons, the diff pane and every hint line. A clean turn is now three lines, and the dot’s color is the verdict. It reads as part of Claude Code, which is what a mod that redraws Claude Code’s rows should do. 5. Make your mod easy to audit To get listed in Claude’s plugin directory, I moved every function that takes $ into the one hooks module. The draw code takes plain values. Now one file holds every call the mod can make, and anyone can check it in a few minutes. 6. Bugs hide in the quiet features My latest fix was not in the row. The context bar kept the old numbers after /compact, because it measured the transcript before the new one was in place. It looked right until the next request, so I didn't see it for days. Image by the author. Try it, or build your own If you want to see a mod that redraws Claude Code’s own rows, install TL;DR inside Claude Code (2.1.301 or later, terminal only): /plugin install tldr --marketplace kushalBanda/claude-tldr The source is on GitHub at kushalBanda/claude-tldr . Read the hooks module and run claude plugin validate on it first. That's the habit I'd want for every mod you install, mine included. If you build your own, start from Anthropic’s mods overview and the three sample mods. Pick one render site and one event, and get a single line on screen. Everything else grows from there. Resources GitHub: https://github.com/kushalBanda/claude-tldr Mods overview, Claude Code Docs: https://code.claude.com/docs/en/plugins/mods/overview Create a mod: https://code.claude.com/docs/en/plugins/mods/create React to events with a mod: https://code.claude.com/docs/en/plugins/mods/events Mods reference: https://code.claude.com/docs/en/plugins/mods/reference TL;DR for Claude Code: https://kushalbanda.com/claude-tldr/?utm_source=medium&utm_medium=social&utm_campaign=claude-tldr What would you build first with a mod? If you found this useful, give it a clap and drop a comment . I’d love to hear your thoughts 🙌 Follow me here on Medium for more Claude Code deep dives, or connect on LinkedIn .   • MCP server: a separate process. Good for giving Claude new tools and data.
  • Mod: functions inside Claude Code. Good for drawing UI, redrawing Claude Code’s own UI, and stepping into a call or a request.

Being inside buys you five things the others can’t do:

  3. Step into a tool call or a model request: hold a call while you ask the user, answer it without running the tool, or send one request to a different model.
  4. Run code on a command: a /command that runs your function at once, with no Claude turn, even while Claude works.
  5. Share data between hooks: one hook counts tool calls, another shows the count beside the spinner.

If a settings hook already does the job, use the settings hook. I needed number 2, so a mod was the only option.

export const register: Register = (on) => {
  on('turn.complete', async ($, e, next) => {
    const r = await next(e)
    if (e.agentId !== undefined) return r  // skip subagent turns
    const { context } = await $.session.usage()
    const secs = Math.round(e.durationMs / 1000)
    return { text: `${secs}s · context ${context.percent}% full` }
  })

claude --plugin-dir .      # run Claude Code with your mod; a save reloads it
claude plugin validate .   # check the manifest and list every hook and call

The reload on save is what makes mods fast to build. I change a render hook, save, and the row redraws in the session I already have open.
