This part matters more than the API. A mod is not sandboxed. Once it loads, it runs with your permissions. It can read and write your files, start programs, make network requests, read your environment variables, see every prompt and tool call, and approve a tool call before you are asked. Turning on Claude Code’s sandbox does not cover it: the sandbox wraps the Bash commands Claude runs, not processes a mod starts.

So before you install a mod, read what it does. Clone it and run claude plugin validate on the folder. The hooks: and calls: lines list every event it handles and every API it calls, without running it. A mod that only draws rows should not list $.http.fetch or $.process.run. If you want to stop all mods, claude --safe-mode turns them off for one session, and "disableAllHooks": true in ~/.claude/settings.json turns them off everywhere.

A worked example: TL;DR for Claude Code

The mod I built is TL;DR for Claude Code. It folds each turn into one row in Claude Code’s own style: the files Claude changed, the tests before and after, and what to check before you trust the result. Every raw line stays one click away. It is free and open source (MIT), and I’m the only author.

Here is how it maps onto the three parts:

  • Events: tool.call reads each call and its result, then passes it on unchanged. turn.start and turn.complete open and close the row. session.compact keeps rows when you run /compact.
  • Render sites: ToolUse and ToolGroup draw the row in place of the tool rows. Spinner names the current job, such as Reading src/auth.py. AbovePrompt draws a context bar. Three Panes hold the detail, the context and the history.
  • $: $.store keeps finished rows (50 per session) and how long each command took last time. $.session.usage feeds the context bar. $.ui.notify pings you when a turn over 30 seconds ends.

The calls it does not make are the point. It makes no $.http or $.model calls and starts no processes. It reads everything from what Claude Code reports.

The row flags the edits that can fake a green run:

Image by the author.What I learned building it1. A static reader misses more than you expect

TL;DR reads each Bash command as text. It never runs or expands a command to learn what it did. I chose that for privacy and safety. The cost showed up fast. I wrote 30 edge cases, and the first version missed many: quoted paths, sudo tee, a cd before a write, mv into a folder, git restore, find -delete, and echo "npm test", which it counted as a test run.

Then a live turn wrote a script with S=/tmp/x.sh; cat > "$S" and the row showed nothing. Now the reader follows variables the command sets. My rule became: name what the text names, and drop what it can't name. A path built from $OUT drops out, because a row that says $OUT via Bash reads like a real file name.

2. A wrapper can hide a failure

I run a hook that wraps test output and prints its own summary line, such as Go test: 20 passed, 2 failed. The first parser didn't know that line. A failing run showed green. Pipes do the same: in go test | tail, the exit code is tail's. Now a failure in the output counts as a failure, whatever the exit code says. If your mod reports test results, test it against the wrappers you actually use.

3. Real data breaks your layout

A flag once quoted a whole heredoc command. The check line was 6,000 characters. Now each flag is one line, cut at the row’s edge, and it names the act, not the command: force push, skipped hooks. The commands behind it open in a pane.

4. Deleting made it look native

The first version was a seven-row box with labels, buttons, a diff pane and hint lines. On a dark terminal the labels were almost invisible, and a 60-file refactor took nine rows of cut-off file names. Version 0.1.5 removed the box, the buttons, the diff pane and every hint line. A clean turn is now three lines, and the dot’s color is the verdict. It reads as part of Claude Code, which is what a mod that redraws Claude Code’s rows should do.

5. Make your mod easy to audit

To get listed in Claude’s plugin directory, I moved every function that takes $ into the one hooks module. The draw code takes plain values. Now one file holds every call the mod can make, and anyone can check it in a few minutes.

6. Bugs hide in the quiet features

My latest fix was not in the row. The context bar kept the old numbers after /compact, because it measured the transcript before the new one was in place. It looked right until the next request, so I didn't see it for days.

Image by the author.Try it, or build your own

If you want to see a mod that redraws Claude Code’s own rows, install TL;DR inside Claude Code (2.1.301 or later, terminal only):

/plugin install tldr --marketplace kushalBanda/claude-tldr

The source is on GitHub at kushalBanda/claude-tldr. Read the hooks module and run claude plugin validate on it first. That's the habit I'd want for every mod you install, mine included.

If you build your own, start from Anthropic’s mods overview and the three sample mods. Pick one render site and one event, and get a single line on screen. Everything else grows from there.

Resources

  • GitHub: https://github.com/kushalBanda/claude-tldr
  • Mods overview, Claude Code Docs: https://code.claude.com/docs/en/plugins/mods/overview
  • Create a mod: https://code.claude.com/docs/en/plugins/mods/create
  • React to events with a mod: https://code.claude.com/docs/en/plugins/mods/events
  • Mods reference: https://code.claude.com/docs/en/plugins/mods/reference
  • TL;DR for Claude Code: https://kushalbanda.com/claude-tldr/?utm_source=medium&utm_medium=social&utm_campaign=claude-tldr

What would you build first with a mod? If you found this useful, give it a clap and drop a comment. I’d love to hear your thoughts 🙌

Follow me here on Medium for more Claude Code deep dives, or connect on LinkedIn.

items.title: Anthropic’s trillion-dollar IPO is open to Australians. There’s a catch for small investors
items.summary: For the second time this year, Wall Street is preparing for a blockbuster stock market debut. Shares in Anthropic – the company behind the Claude artificial intelligence (AI) models – are due to start trading on the US NASDAQ stock exchange on Thursday, US time. Decades of US data show most of the gains from tech floats go to those who are allocated shares at the offer price, and that is rarely small investors. Those who buy only after the shares start trading have tended to do worse. Who makes money from tech floats? An initial public offering, or IPO, is when a private company first sells shares to the public. Australia is one of only a few places outside the US where retail investors can apply. Before trading starts, shares are sold at a fixed “offer price” to investors who applied – mostly big institutional investors, plus some everyday investors through brokers. Once the shares list, anyone can buy them on the stock market, at whatever price buyers and sellers agree on. When demand is strong, that price often jumps. The rise from the offer price to the end of the first day’s trading is known as the “pop”. University of Florida finance professor Jay Ritter has tracked more than 9,000 American floats since 1980. Tech floats have jumped 31% on average between the offer price and the first day’s close. ‘Pops’ and drops In 2020, Wall Street saw a “frenzy” of tech floats, with some extraordinary pops. Shares in Airbnb, for example, more than doubled on day one. Since then, banks have been pricing the biggest deals more cautiously, though average pops remain large. What happens after day one is much less exciting. Leave out the dot-com bubble, and tech shares bought at the offer price beat the US share market by about 26 percentage points over the next three years. Bought at the first day’s closing price, they trailed it by about five percentage points. Almost all the gain was the pop. Informed investors, often big institutions, pile into the good deals and avoid the bad ones. US evidence shows institutions are given more shares in the floats that jump most on day one. Academic research has called the result the “ winner’s curse ”. Small investors only get a sliver of the floats that do well, but everything they asked for in the ones that flop. In addition to the stock market listing, Anthropic has also arranged to sell US$26 billion worth of shares through private placements to Google, Nvidia, Microsoft and other tech giants. And importantly, Anthropic is selling only a small slice of the company. Including the side deal, it is set to raise about US$87 billion, which values the whole company at about US$1.4 trillion once all shares and options are counted. This would slightly exceed the record US$85.7 billion raised by SpaceX in its June float, even though SpaceX’s opening valuation was higher (US$1.77 trillion). Anthropic’s stock market debut this week is set to be among the biggest IPOs in history. NurPhoto/Getty The fine print According to the US prospectus , only about 6% of Anthropic’s shares will be sold in the float. Existing investors and staff hold nearly all the rest and have agreed not to sell for up to a year. Shareholders will have little power, as a trust and a company controlled by the founders are expected to elect the whole board. Anthropic’s revenue rocketed from US$4.6 billion in 2025 to US$33.2 billion in the first nine months of this year. However, the company still made an operating loss of US$1.3 billion . It has also committed to about US$901 billion of future spending, mostly on computing power. There’ll be no dividends for now, so investors only make money if the share price goes up. The shares trade only on Nasdaq and only in US dollars, so currency swings will also impact any returns for Australians. The timing worries some. Anthropic is chasing a record float just as AI funding is starting to dry up , and there are signs investors are already losing faith in the AI story.
items.summary_html:
For the second time this year, Wall Street is preparing for a blockbuster stock market debut. Shares in Anthropic – the company behind the Claude artificial intelligence (AI) models – are due to start trading on the US NASDAQ stock exchange on Thursday, US time.

As with the SpaceX listing earlier this year, everyday Australian investors can be part of the action. They have until 5pm (AEDT) on Tuesday to apply for shares in Anthropic at the offer price.

Doing so doesn’t guarantee they’ll get the full amount they apply for – or any shares at all. According to Bloomberg, bankers say the offer is about six times oversubscribed.

That matters, because who gets shares at the offer price largely decides who makes money. Decades of US data show most of the gains from tech floats go to those who are allocated shares at the offer price, and that is rarely small investors. Those who buy only after the shares start trading have tended to do worse.

Who makes money from tech floats?

An initial public offering, or IPO, is when a private company first sells shares to the public. Australia is one of only a few places outside the US where retail investors can apply.

Anthropic plans to sell 825 million shares at US$70–$78 each (A$104–$115), under the ticker “ANT”.

Not everyone pays the same price, though. Before trading starts, shares are sold at a fixed “offer price” to investors who applied – mostly big institutional investors, plus some everyday investors through brokers. Once the shares list, anyone can buy them on the stock market, at whatever price buyers and sellers agree on.

When demand is strong, that price often jumps. The rise from the offer price to the end of the first day’s trading is known as the “pop”.

University of Florida finance professor Jay Ritter has tracked more than 9,000 American floats since 1980. Tech floats have jumped 31% on average between the offer price and the first day’s close.

‘Pops’ and drops

In 2020, Wall Street saw a “frenzy” of tech floats, with some extraordinary pops. Shares in Airbnb, for example, more than doubled on day one. Since then, banks have been pricing the biggest deals more cautiously, though average pops remain large.

What happens after day one is much less exciting. Leave out the dot-com bubble, and tech shares bought at the offer price beat the US share market by about 26 percentage points over the next three years.

Bought at the first day’s closing price, they trailed it by about five percentage points. Almost all the gain was the pop.

Why small investors miss out

When a float is popular, orders outstrip the number of shares offered and applications get scaled back.

Informed investors, often big institutions, pile into the good deals and avoid the bad ones. US evidence shows institutions are given more shares in the floats that jump most on day one.

Academic research has called the result the “winner’s curse”. Small investors only get a sliver of the floats that do well, but everything they asked for in the ones that flop.

In addition to the stock market listing, Anthropic has also arranged to sell US$26 billion worth of shares through private placements to Google, Nvidia, Microsoft and other tech giants.

And importantly, Anthropic is selling only a small slice of the company. Including the side deal, it is set to raise about US$87 billion, which values the whole company at about US$1.4 trillion once all shares and options are counted.

This would slightly exceed the record US$85.7 billion raised by SpaceX in its June float, even though SpaceX’s opening valuation was higher (US$1.77 trillion).

Anthropic’s stock market debut this week is set to be among the biggest IPOs in history. NurPhoto/Getty The fine print

According to the US prospectus, only about 6% of Anthropic’s shares will be sold in the float. Existing investors and staff hold nearly all the rest and have agreed not to sell for up to a year.

Shareholders will have little power, as a trust and a company controlled by the founders are expected to elect the whole board.

Anthropic’s revenue rocketed from US$4.6 billion in 2025 to US$33.2 billion in the first nine months of this year. However, the company still made an operating loss of US$1.3 billion. It has also committed to about US$901 billion of future spending, mostly on computing power.

There’ll be no dividends for now, so investors only make money if the share price goes up. The shares trade only on Nasdaq and only in US dollars, so currency swings will also impact any returns for Australians.

The timing worries some. Anthropic is chasing a record float just as AI funding is starting to dry up, and there are signs investors are already losing faith in the AI story.

Read more: Shares in this data centre company are down 40% as investors lose faith in the AI story

Keeping a level head

Many investors do little homework. One recent US study of investors’ web browsing found the typical person spends about six minutes researching a stock before trading it, looking mostly at price charts and analysts’ views rather than risk.

Six minutes isn’t much time to size up a loss-making company worth around US$1.4 trillion.

Anthropic may well turn out to be a great company. Whether it’s a good buy is a separate question. History says the gains go mostly to whoever gets in at the offer price, and small investors rarely get much.

items.title: Apple Opens U.S. Study of Trust in Conversational Health AI
items.summary: Apple announced the U.S. launch of the Apple Health AI Usage Study on November 15, 2026, a virtual research project conducted with OpenEvidence and open to as many as 200,000 participants. It will examine trust, response quality, comprehension and everyday health actions when people use conversational health AI. items.title: Apple’s new study looks to improve the effectiveness of AI health tools
items.summary: Apple announced a new study today with the goal of better understanding how people interact with conversational AI health tools and how useful their responses actually are. The company is conducting the Apple Health AI Usage Study in collaboration with OpenEvidence , a clinical AI platform used by healthcare professionals that generates answers based on medical information from sources like The New England Journal of Medicine . Participants will use a new iOS app to ask medical questions and then rate the responses based on criteria including accuracy, detail, and relevance. The app is now available for download, and enrollment starts today, …

items.title: Elon Musk joins 165,000 others calling for Nvidia to bring back Jensen Huang in open letter
items.summary: Silicon Valley figures back CEO ousted after revelations of affair with suspected Chinese spy, as US treasury secretary urges Nvidia to carry out ‘dramatic shake-up’ Elon Musk and a host of other tech executives are among more than 165,000 signatories of an open letter calling for Jensen Huang’s reinstatement as Nvidia chief, days after he resigned from the multi-trillion dollar chip company. The letter demands that the company’s board members “bring Jensen back while an independent investigation establishes the facts”.
items.summary_html:
Silicon Valley figures back CEO ousted after revelations of affair with suspected Chinese spy, as US treasury secretary urges Nvidia to carry out ‘dramatic shake-up’

Elon Musk and a host of other tech executives are among more than 165,000 signatories of an open letter calling for Jensen Huang’s reinstatement as Nvidia chief, days after he resigned from the multi-trillion dollar chip company.

The letter demands that the company’s board members “bring Jensen back while an independent investigation establishes the facts”.
